items.text:
India's Modi government calls special sitting of parliament
Published November 27, 2026last updated November 27, 2026
What you need to know
These are our rolling updates from India on Friday, November 27:
- A brief sitting of the Indian parliament will take place after the monsoon session was adjourned indefinitely back in August
- India's Lok Sabha is set to meet on Monday
- The Rajya Sabha will resume proceedings on Wednesday
How has india's opposition reacted to the reconvening of parliament?
India's main opposition Congress party has deemed the move by Modi's government to call for the brief sitting of the parliament "an assault on the Constitution of India" which Congress General Secretary in-charge Communications and MP Jairam Ramesh said "must and will be resisted with all might."
In a post on X, Ramesh accused the government of "moving to manufacture a fraudulent two-thirds majority in the Lok Sabha"
Ramesh also listed out a three-point Congress stance on delimitation and women's quota, which includes:
- Maintaining the current strength of the Lok Sabha for another 25 years.
- Maintaining the current state-wise distribution of seats in the Lok Sabha for another 25 years
- Implementation of one-third reservation for women and reservation within reservation for women belonging to Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes from the next general elections, slated for 2029.
A meeting of the Congress Parliamentary Strategy Group is also expected to be held on Saturday to discuss the gameplan for the upcoming parliament sitting, news agency ANI reported.
Indian parliament to hold special sitting after a gap of more than 100 days
A political storm could be on the horizon in India as both houses of India's bicameral parliament are set to reconvene next week for a special sitting at the request of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government.
The Lok Sabha (lower house) is slated to sit on November 30 while the Rajya Sabha (upper house) will meet on December 2, official memos said, adding that the session may conclude on December 3.
"The Government has requested Hon'ble Speaker, Lok Sabha and Hon'ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha to reconvene Lok Sabha on Monday, 30th November, 2026 and Rajya Sabha on Wednesday, 2nd December, 2026 respectively to transact essential Government Business," Union Minister of Parliamentary Affairs Kiren Rijiju wrote on X, announcing the government's request on Thursday evening.
The resumption of parliament comes after the monsoon session, which is the second regular session of India's legislative body, saw both the houses being adjourned sine die (indefinitely) on August 13.
The session never ended formally and has remained unprorogued for a record over 100 days, while a winter session that typically starts early December looks delayed.
The monsoon session was turbulent as it began amid a massive youth-led protest called by India's "Cockroach" movement that sought, and later managed to get, the resignation of Modi's then-education minister Dharmendra Pradhan over exam irregularities.
The parliament, itself, became a protest ground as both Modi's ruling coalition, led by his Bharatiya Janata Party, and the opposition INDIA bloc, by Congress, held demonstrations within its premises.
The political deadlock was unrelenting and the parliament struggled to get much business underway, culminating in the adjournment.
Welcome to our coverage
This is Dharvi Vaid Dhulia from DW's bureau in New Delhi, back with your daily dose of news from India.
Here is what's creating a buzz in the world's largest democracy this morning:
Indian lawmakers are making their way back to the parliament next week, more than three months after a rocky — and not formal — conclusion of the monsoon session of the country's supreme legislative body which struggled to conduct its business amid an outpouring of protests against Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government over student issues.
The Modi government's request to reconvene both houses of the parliament for a special sitting has been accepted, with parliamentarians huddling in the Lok Sabha — the lower house — on November 30 and Rajya Sabha — the upper house — on December 2.
The ruling coalition has not explicitly stated what affairs it wants to discuss during the short session and has only said it wants to "transact essential government business."
However, speculation is rife that Modi's government could once again push a package of defeated bills — including a contentious population-based redrawing of voting boundaries and a women's quota intertwined with it.
And in the world of cricket, it is day one of the second test match between India and New Zealand in Christchurch's Hagley Oval . Both teams are vying for a series win in this final match after the first one in Wellington ended in a draw.
Read along for more.

items.text:
What makes or breaks a high press?
- Published
A good high press has been the basis for some of the most successful sides in modern football but a well-oiled pressing machine has many moving parts - all requiring close attention.
When an out-of-possession plan is implemented poorly, entire seasons can fall apart.
So, what determines whether a press works or fails? And how are the always-adapting Premier League teams exploiting high presses this season?
1. Establishing intent
When a team decides to press, they must first establish their intention. This informs how the players act.
Speaking to DAZN Portugal, Brighton manager Fabian Hurzeler was asked about whether a good press relied more on physicality or courage.
"A really good question," he began.
"When you want to press high you need the courage and mindset to do it. Our mindset is we press to score, we don't just press to win the ball back."
In coaching, clarity is key - particularly when it comes to creating alignment in the squad and Hurzeler is deliberate in simplifying big ideas when delivering messages to his players, a skill he practised as a radio pundit during the World Cup.
"[Punditry] helps you as a coach in that you have to summarise things in a short and easy way so that everyone understands," he said. "Football might get more complex but simplicity counts."
Hurzeler's "pressing to score" is a phrase that communicates many ideas in a memorable three words: intensity, being proactive, and immediate forward-thinking on winning the ball.
It also frames pressing in a way that makes it easy for attackers to buy into, in the form of goals.
"You want commitment from everyone on the pitch," Hurzeler explained.
"If just one has doubts, the whole press is gone."
The Red Bull school of coaching uses a similarly succinct phrase - "the last step" to address these ideas around intention, collectiveness and aggression.
Summarised by Tactx, whose coaches have worked under the Red Bull model, the last step refers to "players [being] coached to attack through the opponent, using the final step to lunge aggressively at the ball".
"This action commits the defender fully and is often the decisive moment that allows possession to be won."
Pressing to engage rather than just to close distances ensures the team in possession aren't given the time or space to play through otherwise half-hearted pressure.
1 of 2
2. Knowing when to press and when to drop off
When discussing how good or bad a team is at pressing, how much they run is often brought up. But the distance a team covers fails to paint the full picture when it comes to the effectiveness of a team's pressing strategy.
Liverpool's current boss Andoni Iraola was asked about how he interpreted physical data last year.
"It's not 'we run a lot, so we are good,' no," he said. "The high-speed running, the sprint speeds [matter for us] - not total distance covered.
"[Some] teams that do not run a lot get very good results because they have [their] way of playing."
Sprints matter more than distance covered for Iraola's side, who have clear ideas of how to press, looking to win the ball back through a sudden and intense pressure from familiar positions they are well prepared for.
If the conditions to implement this press aren't on, the wingers can be seen dropping off, forming a more compact defensive shape with the likes of Alexander Isak and Florian Wirtz defending in a front two for longer periods of the match.
It's smart. Liverpool look to maximise the effectiveness of when they do press, with full commitment expected in each sprint, with players conserving their energy in moments a press is less likely to succeed.
With pressing being a front-footed idea, coaches may throw caution to the wind but this can leave them exposed in ways teams have become better at exploiting.
Hurzeler touched on the need for balance when pressing.
"I always say in certain moments you need to have the courage to take risk but you need to have the discipline to control the risk," he said.
For Brighton, this looks like certain players abandoning man-to-man marking when their respective attacker attempts to drag them into awkward positions.
Instead, Brighton will protect the centre of the pitch on top of their man-to-man principles which helps them stay compact.
3. Why compactness is key
When the defending side aren't compact, spaces exist for the attacking side to target. When players step up to press, these gaps can arise in between the lines.
Again, Brighton manage to plug these gaps well by pressing hard, reducing the time opponents have to play passes into midfield, while also encouraging players to make vertical jumps up the pitch, covering players left by teammates who have pressed higher up the pitch.
1 of 2
When teams lack vertical compactness - not pressing with enough intensity and without making the necessary steps up the pitch - the space left in midfield has been exploited by clever sides, such as Leeds.
In their 4-1 loss to Daniel Farke's men, Chelsea looked to press high, with attackers and midfielders running up the pitch to apply pressure.
But when the ball went back the other way, these same players struggled.
The idea behind playing over a team's press isn't always to make the ball stick at the feet of a target man, although this helps. Instead space is found in the gaps between the pressing side's lines.
Recognising when teammates are likely to win headers or clip the ball forwards, midfielders are able to turn and run in the direction the ball is heading in, positioned ready to win second balls in numbers.
By comparison, the pressing side's midfielders, having to apply forward pressure before turning around to track back are often slower to contest second balls.
1 of 4

items.text:
Can the Mecca pact turn its collective defence promise into real support?
Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye meet in Islamabad as Houthi attacks on the kingdom continue and Iran talks stay open.
Islamabad, Pakistan – Senior officials from Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye are meeting in Islamabad on Friday to discuss their Mecca defence pact, as Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and sporadic Iranian strikes on other Gulf countries continue.
The officials are meeting for the third time since the three countries signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement on August 7, under which an armed attack on one member is treated as an attack on all three.
The agreement was signed amid a wider war that began with United States-Israeli strikes on Iran in February.
Pakistan’s Defence Minister Khawaja Asif told the AFP news agency earlier this week that the “continuous turmoil south of Saudi Arabia” – a reference to Yemen, where the Houthis are based – would be on the agenda. He confirmed that the defence and foreign ministers of all three countries would attend the Islamabad meeting.
“Any threat to Saudi Arabia is a threat to Pakistan and Turkiye according to the pact, which is absolutely clear,” Asif said.
He described the pact as still being at an early stage.
“Initially we need to have frequent meetings to steer what is being formulated, in a way that in the next couple of months we have everything in place so that we can move forward,” he said.
Pakistan has pledged to defend Saudi territory but has ruled out attacking the Houthis inside Yemen.
A pledge with limits
Pakistan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs set out that boundary on October 9. Spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan said Pakistani troops stationed in Saudi Arabia under the alliance would not cross into Yemen to attack the Houthis.
“It is an alliance intended to defend the three countries against aggression,” he said at the weekly news briefing.
On April 11, as Islamabad hosted talks between US and Iranian officials aimed at ending the war, Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Defence said a Pakistani force, including fighter and support aircraft, had arrived at King Abdulaziz airbase in the country’s Eastern Province under a bilateral mutual defence agreement that Islamabad and Riyadh had signed in 2025.
Muhammad Faisal, a Sydney-based security and foreign policy analyst, said much of the Pakistani military presence in Saudi Arabia rested on that older bilateral arrangement.
“Importantly, Pakistan’s existing military presence and defence coordination with Saudi Arabia largely predate the Mecca Pact,” he told Al Jazeera, referring to the bilateral mutual defence pact inked in September 2025, at a time when Gulf countries were reevaluating their dependence on US security guarantees after Israel struck Qatar.
Faisal added that Riyadh had not publicly pressed Islamabad to take part in offensive operations inside Yemen.
But Umer Karim, an associate fellow at the King Faisal Center for Research and Islamic Studies in Riyadh, said that limit fell short of what Saudi Arabia wanted.
Therein lies a dilemma, both for Pakistan and for Saudi Arabia: The deeper Pakistan becomes involved against the Houthis, Karim said, the weaker its diplomatic role would become in US-Iran mediation and in its more recent efforts to mediate between Iran and Saudi Arabia. That’s because Iran is the principal external backer of the Houthis.
“Saudi Arabia wants Pakistan to contribute to its defence against the Houthis, and perhaps to act more against the Houthis in an offensive manner, but it also wants to retain Pakistan as a conduit of diplomatic engagement with Iran,” he told Al Jazeera.
Pressure on the ground
On November 24, the Saudi Civil Defence said 11 people were injured when a tower in Riyadh’s financial centre was hit in a Houthi attack.
At least 26 people have been killed in suspected Houthi drone and missile attacks in Saudi Arabia since September 23, according to Saudi authorities. Twenty-three of them were killed in strikes on airports.
At an emergency meeting of the pact’s member countries in Riyadh on October 5, the committee agreed to provide forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the kingdom.
The joint statement did not name Yemen or the Houthis.
On November 21, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan told Turkish media: “Our current policy is aimed at the defence of Saudi Arabia; no decision has been made on deploying troops inside Yemen. However, the necessary support is being provided in defending Saudi Arabia.”
Omer Ozkizilcik, an Ankara-based analyst and nonresident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, expected the alliance to remain defensive for the moment.
“As of now, as the Saudis only requested defensive support, I do not expect the Mecca Pact to get involved in offensive military operations against the Houthi militias in Yemen,” he told Al Jazeera.
Nawaf Obaid, a senior research fellow at the Department of War Studies at King’s College London, outlined the scope of Pakistan’s commitment.
“Pakistan’s military commitment to the defence of Saudi Arabia encompasses capabilities across the land and air domains, including combat aviation, ground formations, integrated air and missile defence, and geospatial intelligence support. Defensive military operations can involve direct combat,” he told Al Jazeera.
Building the alliance
The Riyadh meeting was also attended by retired Lieutenant General Nauman Mahmood, a former three-star Pakistani general, who was appointed earlier in September as the alliance’s first secretary-general for a three-year term.
The secretariat is based in Riyadh, where Mahmood met Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud on November 19 to review efforts to build the alliance’s institutional framework, according to the Saudi Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

items.text:
Almost a million Americans left without power on Thanksgiving as storm sweeps East Coast
Nearly a million people were left without power Thursday after a severe storm lashed the East Coast of the US, tearing up trees and powerlines on Thanksgiving. New York City authorities had been forced to postpone the annual Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade due to the intense winds.
A powerful storm disrupted the Thanksgiving holiday along much of the US East Coast on Thursday, knocking out power to nearly 1 million customers at one point ‌as wind gusts of up to 112kph toppled trees and power lines.
The storm contributed to flight delays, with FlightAware reporting a total of 454 US-related cancellations on Thursday and 2,411 delays. ‌Major airports in the Washington and New York City areas were among the hardest hit.
Heavy rains flooded coastal areas, while utilities warned of an increased risk of falling trees and power outages.
More than 908,000 US utility customers had no power as of 9:56pm ET (0256 GMT), according to PowerOutage.us, down from 961,000 ‌at 7:30pm ET.
The data included more than 207,000 outages in Pennsylvania, over 179,000 in New Jersey, 139,000 in Maryland, 106,000 in Virginia, 100,000 in Missouri and more than 68,000 in New York state.
Wind ‌gusts of 80 to 112kph were reported or forecast across parts of Virginia, Maryland, Delaware, New Jersey, New York, and coastal New England, according to the US National Weather Service.
It said conditions would gradually improve across the Mid-Atlantic overnight as the heaviest rain and strongest winds moved into New England, although blustery conditions with gusts of 40 to 55kph were expected across parts of the East Coast on Friday.
New York City Emergency Management reported winds intensified on Thursday afternoon, reaching 90kph at LaGuardia Airport.
The NWS said strong onshore winds associated with the storm, combined with king tides, were causing coastal flooding in low-lying communities along portions of the East Coast.
Officials had already postponed Thursday's 100th edition of the annual Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York City because of the storm threat, the first time the event has been rescheduled due to severe weather.
People were rescued from their cars in New York City because of flooding, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said, and similar rescues were reported in other coastal communities.
“There is no destination worth your safety,” Mamdani said.
Separately on Thursday, US President Donald Trump said he had approved about $100 million in federal aid to Florida following severe storms and flooding there. He said the total included funding previously approved in connection with Hurricane Isaias.
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters and AP)

items.title: Hakeem Jeffries has disarmed a progressive revolt, but can he deliver?
items.summary:
Hakeem Jeffries has disarmed a progressive revolt, but can he deliver?
The presumptive House speaker’s political pragmatism will be tested by divisions over healthcare, Israel and the war on Iran.
The overwhelming blue wave of the 2026 United States midterm elections should have simply been seen as
items.text:
Hakeem Jeffries has disarmed a progressive revolt, but can he deliver?
The presumptive House speaker’s political pragmatism will be tested by divisions over healthcare, Israel and the war on Iran.
The overwhelming blue wave of the 2026 United States midterm elections should have simply been seen as a crowning achievement for House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries that propelled him into the position of next speaker of the House of Representatives. And while that outcome appears all but guaranteed now that he has secured more than enough support from the incoming House Democratic Caucus, Jeffries’ ascent to the top House leadership position has been significantly rockier than anticipated.
The blue wave was, in part, a progressive and anti-establishment phenomenon. And while we in the media have likely exaggerated the impact of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) in this year’s election cycle, DSA-affiliated and other newly elected far-left lawmakers have already asserted themselves as a vocal minority amongst the incoming House Democratic Caucus. They’ve done so by calling on the party to move left on issues such as healthcare, campaign finance and America’s relationship with Israel. And these newly elected progressives have also targeted congressional leaders, namely Jeffries and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, who they see as embodying the party’s status quo.
Jeffries has reached the pinnacle of power within his party by being a shrewd political operator who has deftly managed the leverage of the Democratic minority in the closely divided House. His handling of the recent challenge to his leadership shows that he remains a step ahead of his opponents within the party. Jeffries declined the opportunity to be chosen by acclamation, an option that could have allowed him to gloss over the opposition to his speakership. Instead, Jeffries insisted on a formal secret ballot. The choice was strategic. Much like a prime minister calling for early elections, he organised the vote to happen before progressive opposition had coalesced around a single candidate (unlike in the Senate, where Maryland’s Chris Van Hollen is amassing support to challenge Schumer). The move represented a tactic Jeffries observed while under the wing of Nancy Pelosi, who called a similar vote in 2018 after her leadership was challenged by vocal incoming members of Congress. In the end, potential challengers for the role of speaker, such as Representatives Ayanna Pressley of Massachusetts and Jamie Raskin of Maryland, declined to throw their hats in the ring to run against Jeffries. The vast majority of the caucus fell in line behind the New York congressman, with 251 votes in favour and only 11 against, the latter largely from incoming DSA-aligned representatives-elect.
For Jeffries, the progressive revolt against his leadership has been, in the short term, a mere speed bump on his path to becoming speaker. In the longer term, those 11 “no” votes represent a more significant progressive challenge to Jeffries’ record and agenda that will not easily disappear. However, the presumptive next speaker of the House is poised to overcome this challenge, as his skill as a political operative, the relatively weak position of his progressive opposition, and the historic nature of Jeffries’ leadership all work in his favour.
Over the course of the 2026 election cycle, Jeffries secured the support of important progressive figures, including fellow New Yorkers such as New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. During the brief post-election speculation over his leadership, the New York congressman also won over progressives including Texas Representative Greg Casar, chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus. Jeffries’ predecessor as Democratic leader, Pelosi, was able to manage dissent from the progressive Squad through a combination of personal relationships and strategic committee assignments that channelled their energies toward oversight of the executive branch. Jeffries may likewise seek to manage the “Bloc”, as the new progressives are being called by some, in similar fashion.
Meanwhile, Jeffries’ primary message since the midterm elections has been one of affordability, a potent message that has resonated with voters across the political spectrum and thus can unite centrists and progressives within the Democratic Party. The speaker-designate has also signalled that he is willing to move in the direction of progressives’ concerns on substantive issues. Most notably, on November 17, the eve of the speaker nomination vote, Jeffries endorsed a plan to expand Medicare by lowering the age of eligibility for older Americans, covering children under 18, and including dental, vision and hearing coverage. This new “Medicare for more” plan, coupled with rolling back Trump-era cuts to Medicaid and restoring Affordable Care Act tax credits, has been gaining steam among both centrists and progressives. The latter have framed it as a quickly achievable first step towards Medicare for All. Both progressive elder statesman Senator Bernie Sanders and members of the Congressional Progressive Caucus have adopted this rhetoric.
Whether this “first step” framing is accurate is unknowable. The Affordable Care Act was presented in similar terms, but the progressive aim to use Obamacare as a foundation to build a universal healthcare system did not materialise over the subsequent decade. However, the willingness of major progressive forces to adopt the narrative seems to be opening space for Jeffries to navigate. This undercuts the power that the incoming progressives have to make healthcare a major dividing issue within the Democratic caucus.
Jeffries also has the power of history on his side. The congressman from Brooklyn is poised to take control of the top House spot as the chamber’s first Black speaker. He will be backed by an unprecedented slate of diverse leaders within the Democratic House Cauc

items.title: Western sanctions on Israeli settlers serve to shield the Israeli state
items.summary:
Western sanctions on Israeli settlers serve to shield the Israeli state
The takeover of Palestinian homes in Jericho exposes the futility of sanctions that leave Israel’s settler-colonial system intact.
On November 17, a 72-year-old Palestinian woman, Fadda Fheidat, was shot in the head and killed a
items.text:
Western sanctions on Israeli settlers serve to shield the Israeli state
The takeover of Palestinian homes in Jericho exposes the futility of sanctions that leave Israel’s settler-colonial system intact.
On November 17, a 72-year-old Palestinian woman, Fadda Fheidat, was shot in the head and killed as she stood outside her home in al-Duyuk at-Tahta in Jericho. Fadda was murdered by Israeli settlers, who had recently forcibly evicted at least 13 Palestinian households from their homes in the neighbourhood.
What makes this takeover so significant is the location: the outskirts of Jericho, widely described as the world’s oldest continuously inhabited city and the first city to be handed over to the newly established Palestinian Authority in 1994 following the Oslo Accords.
Hours after Fadda was killed, Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich visited the new settlement outpost and praised the settlers for what he characterised as a renewal of Jewish settlement in Jericho. It is the first Israeli settlement established inside a Palestinian city in the West Bank since settlers established a presence in the heart of Hebron nearly five decades ago.
This latest settler takeover was spearheaded by the far-right settler organisation Nachala with the support of the settler Binyamin Regional Council. Nachala was founded by the fanatical settler Daniella Weiss and has long campaigned for the ethnic cleansing and settlement of all of historic Palestine. Weiss and her organisation have gained international notoriety as a result of their relentless campaign calling for the Israeli government to complete the mass expulsion of Palestinians from Gaza and settle the area with Israelis.
Albeit politically significant, the takeover of homes in Jericho is not surprising. Since the genocide in Gaza began more than three years ago, Israeli settler takeover of Palestinian homes and land has drastically escalated in the West Bank. More than 6,000 Palestinians – half of whom are children – have been forcibly expelled as a result. The Israeli military has also been conducting its own expulsions. Between January and February 2025, the Jenin, Nur Shams and Tulkarem refugee camps in the northern West Bank were emptied of their populations – some 33,000 residents.
One cannot separate the actions of the settlers and the military. The two work hand in glove towards their ultimate goal, which is to force as many Palestinians as possible off the land.
Both actors are part of a larger settler-colonial structure which enables this accelerating expansion. Indeed, the majority of settlements in the West Bank are connected to Israeli regime infrastructure, including Israeli-only roads and water and electricity networks, and many offer state subsidies as incentives for Jewish Israelis to live there. When one sees the settlements with one’s own eyes, it is clear that there is no separation between them and the Israeli state.
Yet the distinction between settlers and the settler-colonial structure is a useful tool for Israel’s more liberal supporters. To blame the settlers and a few more extreme ministers is to provide a scapegoat for the structure that masquerades as the only liberal democracy in the region.
We can see this scapegoating in how some Western governments have responded to settlement expansion. For example, both Nachala and Weiss have been sanctioned by the UK, Australia, Canada and the European Union – sanctions that include asset freezes and travel bans. Sanctions like this effectively allow governments to claim action, when in reality, the impact on the ground is limited.
This distinction between settlers and the Israeli regime is also evident in the language used to announce the sanctions. In her November 18 statement announcing the sanctions, Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong failed to mention the Israeli government at all: “We are taking these actions because the rapid expansion of settlements and settler violence are extinguishing the possibility of a two-state solution”.
Some might argue that freezing settler assets and imposing travel bans is at least a step in the right direction. But this is a naive outlook. Limited sanctions like these are a politically calculated tactic. In the UK, growing anger among the British public over their government’s complicity in the genocide necessitated a response from the incoming prime minister, Andy Burnham.
Yet when his foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, announced earlier this year the new approach the UK government was taking vis-à-vis Palestine and Israel, it was reported that British officials were also working to de-escalate tensions and give assurances to the Israeli government that the sanctions would be limited in scope.
Indeed, the earlier sanctions did nothing to stop what happened in al-Duyuk at-Tahta, where Palestinians were evicted from their homes by settlers, supported by soldiers and praised by government ministers. In fact, the settler movement appears to be intact and growing in support and power every day.
This is why sanctions cannot be limited to individual actors and organisations – they need to be comprehensively applied to the structure behind them. But that requires a moral backbone and political courage – something that seems to be completely lacking on the international stage.

What happens now for Bayern Munich and Musiala?
- Published
Bayern Munich - and representatives of one of their most prominent players -have collided over recent weeks.
During the summer, the public became aware that their star 23-year-old midfielder Jamal Musiala suffered from absence seizures.
This neurological condition causes a brief, sudden lapse in awareness and responsiveness. Musiala had two of these lapses during pre-season games, but episodes already happened during the previous year.
At first, the shock among fans and observers was huge. Bayern kept Musiala's condition a secret for some time, and only a few insiders knew about it. In the days after Musiala's lapse during a friendly against Heidenheim, speculations arose over whether the player's medical issue had been known before he signed a highly lucrative contract extension in February 2025.
But it has been confirmed by sources close to the team - and Bayern themselves - that the condition had not been detected before April 2025. One source described Musiala, at the time of signing his new contract, as being "in great health".
In April 2025, days after suffering a muscle tear, Musiala caused a high-speed car crash which cost him his driver's licence. Munich's public prosecutor's office responded to a recent enquiry saying there is no evidence that the accident was caused by a lapse, nor that it was the cause of Musiala's condition.
Nevertheless, checks a couple of days after the crash revealed he was suffering from absence seizures. Musiala's camp consulted numerous experts and hired doctors to treat the player, with the knowledge of Jochen Hahne, Bayern's team doctor. How close the consultations between the external doctors and Bayern's medical staff are remains a point of discussion, among many other things in this complex matter.
Soon after, Musiala's football-related injuries became an issue. He broke his fibula and injured his ankle during the Fifa Club World Cup after colliding with then PSG goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma. He needed months to recover and suffered a subsequent ankle injury, likely related to the leg injury.
After the 2026 World Cup he had a metal plate removed from his left foot, which affected his pre-season preparation. Musiala just recently recovered from a weeks-long absence due to a hamstring tear.
On top of that, new incidents related to his neurological condition have come to light. Days before his recent return to training Musiala had another lapse, just like he did on the morning of a Champions League game against Real Madrid in April.
All of this is the tragic story of a highly talented footballer who might never return to his previous level and must deal with a medical condition for the rest of his life.
Absence seizures require daily medication. There are other high-level athletes, such as England rugby union player Tommy Freeman, who have had to deal with the same condition.
Rummenigge goes on the offensive
A controversy erupted last Friday, as Bayern faced Cologne in what was supposed to be an ordinary league game. Karl-Heinz Rummenigge, once chairman of the board and now a member of Bayern's supervisory board, asked a TV crew to come to his section in the stands.
The unscheduled post-game interview unfolded in a way that no-one at Bayern, not even other members of the club's hierarchy, expected.
"He has a health issue, which is known, and it is known that he has a contract which includes hefty sums of money," Rummenigge said. "You need to talk to the family, to the player and most importantly to the agency, because these sums are - with all due respect - not justifiable any longer."
A day later, chairman of the board Jan-Christian Dreesen and club president Herbert Hainer tried to defuse the situation at the yearly membership assembly, but were also attacked by club member Jonathan Hoffmann.
Hoffmann, a neurologist, said it wouldn't help to go after Musiala publicly, for which he received applause from many of the present members.
One might wonder why an experienced deal-maker like Rummenigge would willingly put down one of his players who could still be valuable to the club, even if it's just for a sale.
He might have been agitated by the way the home game against Cologne went. Harry Kane suffered a ligament tear in his ankle early in the game and star winger Michael Olise had to leave the stadium on crutches.
But, even more importantly, it has become clear that Rummenigge was unhappy with how contract negotiations with Musiala's camp - between October 2024 and February 2025 - unfolded.
Bayern and particularly Max Eberl, the club's director of sport, were running out of time, as Musiala's contract would have ended with the conclusion of the 2025-26 season. If they hadn't reached an agreement before April or May 2025, Bayern would have felt obliged to sell Musiala during the summer transfer window.
Bayern under pressure during contract negotiations
Musiala played an impressive Euro 2024 for Germany and was one of Bayern's best players during the period of negotiations. Among others, Real Madrid were interested, but only for a free transfer in 2026.
Keep in mind, Musiala has quite a unique profile as a No 10 that can also come from the wing and break down low-block defences with his dribbles and passing.
Under pressure and confronted by a shrewd negotiator in Christian Schmid, Musiala's agent and a trained lawyer, Bayern agreed to a salary package that could earn Musiala, in a best-case scenario, £21m a year, with £15m as a base salary. Bayern also agreed to grant a signing fee of close to £25m, paid over the stretch of the contract. Musiala even got his wish granted of receiving his own box at Allianz Arena.

items.text:
Messi confirms Tevez testimonial as Ronaldo showdown in offing
Argentina footballer Lionel Messi confirms testimonial game for Carlos Tevez, with Cristiano Ronaldo role also sought.
Lionel Messi will play in former Argentina teammate Carlos Tevez’s testimonial match on December 20, organisers have confirmed.
Tevez, nicknamed “Apache”, retired in 2022, bringing the curtain down on a career that included stints at Manchester City, Manchester United and Juventus.
The 42-year-old, who ended his ‌career at boyhood club Boca Juniors, said last year he wanted Messi and former Manchester United teammate Cristiano Ronaldo to play in opposing teams in his testimonial.
“It will be a true honour to welcome the best player in the world to Apache’s last dance,” organisers posted on Instagram on Thursday.
Rio Ferdinand, Sergio Aguero, Leandro Paredes, Gianluigi Buffon and Martin Palermo are among the other players ‌confirmed for the match, which will take place at Boca ‌Juniors’ ‌La Bombonera stadium.
Messi and Ronaldo last faced each other in a competitive match in 2020 when representing Barcelona and Juventus, respectively.
The pair also played in an exhibition match when Messi’s Paris Saint-Germain faced a Riyadh Season XI in 2023 following Ronaldo’s move to the Saudi Pro League.
Messi and Inter Miami to dig deep in MLS at Columbus
Meanwhile, with the season and defence of ‌the MLS Cup title on the line, Inter Miami coach Cristian “Kily” Gonzalez believes in his players heading into Game 2 of the best-of-three Eastern Conference series at the Columbus Crew on Friday.
“There are moments when you have to dig deep, tap into that sense of self-respect and the passion that drives you,” he told the media in Spanish on Wednesday. “That’s how I see the game, and I truly hope we can demonstrate that this Friday.”
The No 2 seed Herons have no choice after a 3-0 home loss to the No 7 Crew on Saturday has them facing a first-round exit for the second time in three seasons.
Game 3, if necessary, will be on Wednesday in Miami.
Miami will receive ‌a cold reception in Columbus not only because of a forecasted temperature in the upper 30s with a chance of snow flurries.
During the Crew’s 2-1 win on September 27, Miami was issued five of the nine yellow cards and the lone red card.
On a throw-in during Game 1, Lionel Messi threw the ball into the face of Gonzalo Tapia. Both received cautions.
Crew interim coach Laurent Courtois felt Messi deserved more than a yellow card.
“There’s multiple ways to see that (situation),” Courtois said on Monday. “If you talk about purely the soccer part, I think when he dove inside of our box [earlier in the game], it should’ve been a yellow to start with. And this incident is not only the [throw-in]. It’s the whole sequence that leads to it, and you can tell that there’s weird intentions at the least, so it is what it is.”
There were 36 fouls on Saturday – 22 by Miami – and the Herons had five yellows and one damning red card.
After Tapia put the Crew ahead 1-0 on a penalty kick in the ninth minute, Gonzalo Lujan picked up his second yellow in the 36th ‌and the Crew got goals from Taha Habroune (52nd) and Tapia (58th). Lujan is suspended for Friday’s match.
“I believe the squad are at a point where we understand that it’s time to deliver,” ‌Miami ‌forward Luis Suarez said. “This is our final opportunity. This format has given us another chance to play this Friday, and it’s the last shot we have to bring the series back home.”

Israel's former military chief Gadi Eisenkot on Thursday struck a coalition deal with Yair Golan's left-leaning Democrats, bringing the country's opposition closer to forming a government after no single bloc secured a majority in t
items.text:
Israel's Eisenkot agrees to coalition deal with left-wing Democrats
Israel's former military chief Gadi Eisenkot on Thursday struck a coalition deal with Yair Golan's left-leaning Democrats, bringing the country's opposition closer to forming a government after no single bloc secured a majority in the October elections.
The centrist party of former Israeli military chief Gadi Eisenkot, who is trying to form the next Israeli government, and an allied left-wing party on Thursday announced they had agreed on a coalition deal.
The left-leaning Democrats are the second party to agree to a coalition deal with Eisenkot's Yashar after the right-wing Israel Beiteinu party, headed by Avigdor Lieberman, did so on Tuesday, marking a further step towards forming a government.
Eisenkot has until December 6 – a deadline which can be extended by 14 days – to form a government to replace caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu after the October election failed to deliver a clear majority for either bloc.
"Gadi Eisenkot, chair of Yashar with Eisenkot, and Yair Golan, chair of the Democrats, have agreed to sign a coalition agreement between the two parties," a joint statement said on Thursday.
The Democrats said they would receive four ministerial portfolios as part of the coalition deal, including an expanded national security ministry which under Netanyahu's government is headed by the far-right Itamar Ben-Gvir.
Watch moreWriter Etgar Keret: 'The Israel my parents dreamed of' is still possible, but not under Netanyahu
The party will also receive the Ministry of Labour, Ministry of Communications, and Ministry of Culture and Sport, which will include a new directorate for democracy, the party said in a statement.
"We promised the people that we would replace Netanyahu and defend democracy. And that is what we will do," Golan said in ‌a post on X.
"I call on all parties to come together as soon as possible to finalise agreements and sign them, form a government, and lead Israel in a new direction. This is the mission of our lives."
Eisenkot, Lieberman and Golan have a combined total of 36 lawmakers – far short of the 61 needed for a parliamentary majority.
The bloc also includes the Beyachad party of former prime minister Naftali Bennett, which has 12 seats but is yet to sign a formal coalition agreement with Yashar.
Divided bloc
Eisenkot's wide-ranging anti-Netanyahu camp has faced divisions on whether to forge alliances with the ultra-Orthodox parties, or the Arab-majority lists, or whether to form a national unity government with Netanyahu's right-wing Likud.
The Democrats have been pushing Eisenkot for an alliance with two Arab-majority lists that achieved an unprecedented seat haul in the vote, in a bid to unseat Netanyahu.
The party disapproved of the four rounds of talks between Yashar and Likud in recent days exploring the possibility of a unity government. No breakthroughs on that front have ostensibly been reached.

Lieberman, on the other hand, has refused to serve in a government that relies on Arab-majority parties and has instead advocated an alliance with the two ultra-Orthodox parties, despite his years of criticism of the community and the fact that the issue of ultra-Orthodox military conscription remains a thorny one.
On Thursday, Lieberman warned that Netanyahu was trying to derail the government's formation.
"He will drag out negotiations over a 'unity' government until the last moment, look for a pretext to blow them up, and even if such a government is formed, he will try to engineer a crisis within a few months to drag Israel back to elections," added Lieberman, a hawkish former aide to Netanyahu who has become a strident critic.
Bennett, meanwhile, has been pushing for a unity government between Eisenkot's bloc and Likud that would exclude the ultra-Orthodox and Arab parties.
"Even at this time, I believe that by far the best alternative for the State of Israel and the serving public is a Zionist unity government led by Eisenkot first," he wrote on X, referring to a possible rotation agreement for the premiership.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP and Reuters)

Manchester City's owners must be forced to sell up as punishment for breaking financial rules, senior figures at Premier League clubs have told BBC Sport.
This week, the chair of the Independent Football Regulator (IFR) Davi
items.text:
Man City owners should be forced to sell, say rival club chiefs
- Published
Manchester City's owners must be forced to sell up as punishment for breaking financial rules, senior figures at Premier League clubs have told BBC Sport.
This week, the chair of the Independent Football Regulator (IFR) David Kogan claimed he has the "stomach" to take action against City, who deny wrongdoing and have appealed.
The IFR has the power to remove directors of a club if they are deemed unsuitable, and even force a sale in the most serious cases.
Now, executives at three top-flight rivals have told the BBC that they believe this is the appropriate punishment for City, who were found guilty of breaching Premier League financial regulations rules between 2009 and 2018, and failing to co-operate with an investigation.
- Premier League clubs to cover legal costs if Man City sponsors sue 
  - Published19 November
- Rival clubs want range of punishments for Man City 
  - Published6 October
The independent commission has yet to decide on a sanction that could range from a fine, to a points deduction, the stripping of past titles, or even expulsion from the league.
But speaking on condition of anonymity, one executive claimed they are among a group of clubs who feel that City's punishment will be irrelevant unless the owners are also forced to sell. They added that anything less will make them question why they are funding the regulator through a levy.
In comments that reveal the level of anger felt by some of City's rivals, another claimed the rule breaches had undermined the league's credibility, and that they would not be able to draw a line under the scandal and move on if the owners were allowed to stay. The club were found guilty of inflating revenues and disguising losses by £900m through "sham" commercial arrangements.
Manchester City's owners are Abu Dhabi United Group - a private investment company belonging to United Arab Emirates vice-president and deputy Prime Minister Sheikh Mansour.
The executive who spoke anonymously said that clubs had been asked by the Premier League to refrain from publicly revealing their views on sanctions, and let the process run its course, although some are said to have privately made their opinions clear to IFR officials. They acknowledged that some clubs were less opinionated about a punishment.
Other clubs the BBC approached declined to comment, or said they were willing for the independent commission panel and IFR to reach their own conclusions following the publication of the commission's ruling in September.
But the fact that some clubs want the unprecedented sanction of a forced sale will put pressure on Kogan to mete out the harshest penalty possible in what is being seen as a defining test of the watchdog just over a year after it was established.
It also comes amid mounting questions over whether wider UAE trade and investment in UK projects could be impacted by such a move. In September, Prime Minister Andy Burnham was criticised for saying he would be "really concerned" if the scandal led to City's owners selling the club, adding that "they have been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester".
When approached, the IFR declined to comment. But Kogan has consistently said that the IFR will not be influenced by any political pressure.
Earlier this week he told a parliamentary committee that the watchdog would not be afraid to investigate City's hierarchy and take action, depending on the outcome of the appeal.
"Forget the name of the club, forget the size of the club, forget the scale of the issue. We cannot simply ignore our statutory duties in relation to a club because it happens to be of a certain size," Kogan said.
"We absolutely will have to take the appropriate action as laid out in the legislation, depending on the circumstances as they come to us, which are the evidence that's been presented and collated by the independent commission of the Premier League and by any judgement that takes place on that evidence through an appeal.
"But in one sense, the evidence has already been judged by those cases having been found guilty, so we will absolutely have the stomach to do so... assuming those circumstances are triggered, if we don't act, what is the purpose of having a football regulator?"
When asked how any potential legal battles with Manchester City would be paid for, IFR chief executive Richard Monks told MPs that a litigation reserve of £2m was to be built up over the next two years via the levy charged to clubs, which would be paid back if litigation was successful.
"Now clearly - and I'm not talking about a specific case - clearly, there could be a very large legal case of any particular club that would require us to spend more than £2m in terms of litigation costs and barrister costs in particular", Monks added. "So if that happens, we have agreed with government [that it] will effectively lend us the money in terms of cash flow.
"We'd expect to win that litigation, to claim costs and repay government. If we failed in that massive litigation, then ultimately it would be added to the levy and we'd repay government that way."
Last month it was revealed that the IFR would cost clubs in the top five divisions of English men's football £20.3m annually.
Last week, Premier League clubs voted to cover legal expenses for its five board directors if any of City's sponsors sued them. Two UAE-based commercial partners - Etihad and Etisalat - have both said they are considering legal action against the Premier League.
The IFR has the authority to force a sale within section 34 of the Football Governance Act which allows it to investigate whether an owner meets the required suitability standards around honest, integrity and financial soundness. If an owner fails this assessment, the regulator can direct them to take reasonable steps to relinquish ownership within a specified period before issuing an ownership removal order.

items.summary:
French, Bulgarian presidents slam Marseille violence, five fans in hospital
French and Bulgarian presidents slam Marseille fans after violent scenes in UEFA Europa League match with Levski Sofia.
Five Levski Sofia supporters were taken to hospital after violence ahead of the Europa League game at Ma
items.text:
French, Bulgarian presidents slam Marseille violence, five fans in hospital
French and Bulgarian presidents slam Marseille fans after violent scenes in UEFA Europa League match with Levski Sofia.
Five Levski Sofia supporters were taken to hospital after violence ahead of the Europa League game at Marseille on Thursday, with the French and Bulgarian presidents blaming the home fans.
The lead-up to the match at the Stade Velodrome was marred by confrontations in the stands between the two sets of fans, including the throwing of projectiles and flares.
French President Emmanuel Macron condemned “in the strongest possible terms … acts of violence targeting Bulgarian fans”, the Elysee Palace said.
Bulgarian President Iliana Iotova called it “unacceptable” and “shocking”.
“The attacks against the Bulgarian fans desecrate one of the great games that brings millions of people together around the world,” she said in a statement on Facebook.
“Everyone should be able to support their team without being afraid for their safety.”
Macron spoke to his Bulgarian counterpart on the sidelines of a European summit in Brussels, assuring her that “these acts would not go unpunished”, the Elysee said.
Several hundred Marseille fans ran from the stand where they were situated about 10 minutes before kick-off, appearing to pursue a group of Levski supporters.
They breached the stand designated for away fans, where about 500 visiting fans were gathered.
Fighting broke out, with several Marseille fans wearing face coverings.
“Five people were taken to hospital with eye injuries, head trauma and a dislocated shoulder,” a source with the Marseille police prefecture told the AFP news agency.
“Six others were treated on site for various wounds.”
The police source said all the people injured were Bulgarian and there was “no information at this stage regarding any arrests”.
Manuel Bompard, an MP for the hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) party for Marseille’s Bouches-du-Rhone department, commented on a video shared online purporting to show a Levski fan performing a Nazi salute.
“The far right has no place in our stadiums!” he wrote on X.
Iotova called on French authorities to “clarify the circumstances surrounding the attacks and look for responsibility from those who committed them”.
She urged European football’s governing body UEFA to “check how the safety of the Bulgarian fans at the stadium was ensured”.
“We are ready to provide the necessary assistance to our compatriots. This behaviour is unacceptable!” she said.
Security personnel eventually restored calm as the game kicked off on time.
Another flare-up between opposing fans occurred at halftime, before the match ended 1-0 to the hosts.
“It’s a very regrettable episode – these are incidents which are unacceptable for football,” said Levski coach Julio Velazquez.
“I support the fans who were caught up in this incident. I hope nothing serious has happened. I’m very saddened by this situation.”
Ligue 1 club Marseille said it was “working to understand the precise circumstances of these incidents”.
“We are living through violent times in our society, so this is very, very regrettable,” said Marseille coach Bruno Genesio.

items.title: ‘You can’t stop it’: Indians embrace Pakistani dramas, defying bans
items.summary:
‘You can’t stop it’: Indians embrace Pakistani dramas, defying bans

When New Delhi-based cultural impresario and curator Abu Sufiyan Kh
items.text:
‘You can’t stop it’: Indians embrace Pakistani dramas, defying bans
India has tried to keep Pakistani dramas off its screens since May 2025. Indians get enough of these shows – VPNs and private screenings are coming to their rescue.
When New Delhi-based cultural impresario and curator Abu Sufiyan Khan organised a recent screening of the Pakistani romantic drama Dar-e-Nijaat in the Indian capital, he was stunned. It was meant to be a private event for 45 people, at most. Khan got more than 700 requests for attendance.
Like all other Pakistani shows and songs, Dar-e-Nijaat is officially banned in India. Yet every weekend, Indian viewers gather on Instagram to exchange clips, debate episodes and celebrate its leading character, Abu Bakr.
Offline, watch parties and group screenings are organised in different parts of the country. As the craze for the show – which involves a young woman Zaryab, her childhood love Zamil, and Abu Bakr, who later steps into Zaryab’s life to fill a void – has gripped Indian cities, the police have been left playing cat-and-mouse.
At least two screenings in the southern city of Bengaluru, scheduled for this coming weekend, have now been cancelled after authorities saw posters advertising the events. But those attempts at a crackdown haven’t dimmed the appeal of the show.
One phrase, repeated across fan pages and comment sections, has become a shorthand for its craze: “Sabr ka phal nahi, Abu Bakr chahiye,” (We don’t want the reward of patience; we want Abu Bakr.)
It is a playful twist on a familiar Urdu proverb, and an indication of the affection Indian viewers have developed for a fictional Pakistani man. “We have all been looking forward to an Abu Bakr. I have been going gaga over him because of how empathetic he is, and that is what is missing in most of the men these days,” says Rakhshanda Mujib, a fan from Bengaluru.
Yet the excitement over Dar-e-Nijaat is only the latest expression of a much wider appetite. India’s efforts to keep Pakistani entertainment off its screens have done little to extinguish the appetite for it.
“Indians cannot approach Pakistani artists on Instagram, access Pakistani music on Spotify or view Pakistani dramas without VPNs or proxies on YouTube,” Sufiyan Khan said.
But for many, the forbidden fruit of Pakistani culture remains alluring enough to risk breaching the official ban.
The ban
Despite multiple wars and near-perpetual tensions, India and Pakistan had for decades allowed cultural exchanges – even though they each periodically imposed restrictions.
But informal bans on Pakistani artistes working or performing in India gained ground over the past decade as Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government in New Delhi increasingly dialled down all contact with Pakistan to a bare minimum.
A new tipping point arrived in April 2025, when gunmen killed 26 tourists in Pahalgam, in Indian-administered Kashmir. India blamed Pakistan for the attack, while Islamabad denied any role. The neighbours fought an intense four-day war before agreeing to a ceasefire.
Since then, India has banned all Pakistani songs, movies and dramas from streaming platforms, including YouTube. It has cited national security for its decision. This week, it demanded that Netflix take down – from viewing in India – Pakistan’s first show on that platform.
Yet while China imposed a similar ban on Korean pop culture in 2016, and it held for the better part of a decade, India’s efforts appear to be failing.
The reason lies in where the chokepoint sits. China controls the platforms its citizens use. India does not control YouTube. Section 69A of India’s Information Technology Act lets the government direct platforms to block content, and the orders are generally confidential. In practice, YouTube geo-blocked Pakistani channels for users in India.
But a geo-block governs a platform, not a viewer. A VPN changes where a viewer appears to be, and anyone who downloads a drama that way can re-upload it from an account inside India.
On May 8, 2025 – the day streaming platforms were told to drop Pakistani content – searches for VPNs in India rose 72 percent, according to the monitoring firm Top10VPN, which links the rise to both governments blocking each other’s online content.
The love
Those VPNs downloaded in India translate into good business for Pakistani channels like ARY Digital, the network behind Dar-e-Nijaat.
“Indian viewers account for 30 to 35 percent of total views for Pakistani channels”, says Jerjees Seja, head of ARY Entertainment. “In this day and age, you can make access to content difficult, but you can’t stop it.”
Seja’s assertion is hard to dispute. The 2022 drama Tere Bin and the 2024 soap Kabhi Main Kabhi Tum were both also wildly popular in India. Pakistani director Mehreen Jabbar says viewers in India message her about her series such as Dr Bahu, Jackson Heights and Daam.
So, what makes these shows click for Indian audiences?
Culturally, the similarities between India and Pakistan mean that a lot that’s seen in Pakistani shows is instantly relatable for many across the border. Seja adds that Pakistan’s entertainment industry has also grown in its quality of production. “Our content has become very strong over the years,” he said. “It is realistic, on-the-ground, thought-provoking, and relatable.”
But there’s another reason, too, suggests Sufiyan Khan, that dramas like Dar-e-Nijaat find a willing audience in India. Far too often, Indian shows and movies stereotype Muslim characters. By contrast, Dar-e-Nijaat’s appeal, he said, lies in part in its “exceptional portrayal of Islam as not being threatening or Bollywood-style performative with kohl eyes and prayer caps but a refreshing, non-judgmental and inclusive Islam where all the rituals are being practised with humility”.
The future
Culture is inconvenient in wartime politics because it makes an enemy familiar. But technology has made it harder for governments to firewall entire societies.

His son, Devin Talbott
items.text:
Strobe Talbott, former Time magazine reporter and deputy secretary of state, has died
Strobe Talbott, a former Time magazine reporter who later served as deputy secretary of state under President Bill Clinton and then headed the Brookings Institution, died Thursday. He was 80.
His son, Devin Talbott, confirmed he passed away peacefully after a long illness in his East Hampton, New York, home.
The elder Talbott was educated at Yale and Oxford, where he bunked with Clinton. While at the British university, after interning for Time in Moscow, the magazine asked Talbott to help translate the leaked memoirs of Nikita Khrushchev, the former first secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union who was ousted in 1964.
Talbott did, and it gave him some notoriety as a young man and a job at the magazine.
After 21 years at Time, where he focused on Soviet-American relations and held positions including Washington bureau chief and a foreign-affairs columnist, according to his U.S. State Department biography, he received a call from the newly elected Clinton.
Talbott joined the U.S. State Department in 1994, swiftly becoming deputy secretary of state. In that role, he was the architect of the Clinton administration's approach to Russia and other formerly Soviet countries and conducted negotiations between the U.S. and India after the latter's nuclear tests in 1998.
"Strobe was a good and brilliant man who made our world more peaceful and secure," said Clinton in a statement after Talbott's death. When Talbott was translating Khrushchev's memoirs while at Oxford, it was Clinton's job to make him breakfast every day, he said, adding, "somehow, I got the better end of the deal."
Both he and Hillary were "deeply saddened" by the passing of "a wonderful friend, and a world-class human being," he said.
Afterward, he served as the president of Brookings from 2002 to 2017. In that time, he also chaired the U.S. State Department's Foreign Affairs Policy Board.
Talbott also authored over a dozen books. His last book was titled "Our Founders' Warning: The Age of Reason Meets the Age of Trump," which was published in 2020.
He was born in Dayton, Ohio, in 1946, and is survived by two sons, Devin and Adrian, and six grandchildren.
His first wife, Brook Shearer, died in 2009, and he later married author Barbara Lazear Ascher.

items.text:
Buffalo Bills 13-10 Kansas City Chiefs: Tyler Bass hits 57-yard field goal in final seconds to snatch victory over NFL rivals
Buffalo Bills beat rivals Kansas City Chiefs thanks to a 57-yard field goal from Tyler Bass; he also hit a 54-yard field goal to level the game with 12 minutes remaining
Friday 27 November 2026 06:29, UK
Tyler Bass hit a 57-yard field goal on the hooter as Buffalo Bills improved their AFC-leading record to 10-1 with a 13-10 victory over rivals Kansas City Chiefs.
James Cook had 117 yards rushing and scored on a five-yard run and Bass also made a 54-yard field goal in the defensive struggle.
The highly anticipated fireworks between Buffalo's Josh Allen and Kansas City's Patrick Mahomes, two of the NFL's best quarterbacks, and top offenses failed to materialise.

Allen finished 10 of 21 for 81 yards with two interceptions - both coming inside the Kansas City 20. Mahomes finished 16 of 29 for 174 yards.
Buffalo have won seven straight and matched their best start to a season since 1991.
Emmett Johnson had 72 yards rushing and scored on a one-yard run for the Chiefs.
Neither offense could muster much momentum with rain falling through the evening and cold gusts that made it feel like -5.
Bass's decisive kick came after the Chiefs went three-and-out at their own 11 with 15 seconds remaining. Matt Araiza's punt was partially tipped by Joe Andreessen, leading to a line-drive ball fielded by Greg Dortch, who returned it 17 yards to Kansas City's 39 with four seconds remaining.
Bass's 54-yard field goal to tie it at 10 some 12 minutes earlier also was struck in the same direction.
Kansas City's Harrison Butker, kicking in the other direction toward the north end of the stadium, missed a go-ahead 46-yard attempt wide right with just over five minutes remaining.
In their seventh regular-season meeting since 2020, the Bills improved to 6-1, including six straight wins over Kansas City. The Chiefs, however, hold a 4-0 edge in the playoffs, including two AFC championship game wins.
After Cook opened the scoring 28 seconds into the second quarter, Allen squandered a chance to build a 14-0 lead on the Bills next possession. Facing second-and-eight at the Chiefs nine, Allen rolled to his right, appeared to have his pass slightly tipped by George Karlaftis, and intercepted by Alohi Gilman in the end zone.
It marked the first time in 43 drives inside an opponent's 20 the Bills failed to come away with points this season.
He would turn it over again in the red zone two drives later on Buffalo's first possession of the second half. On first-and-10 at Kansas City's 14, Allen's sidearm pass to Khalil Shakir was low, glanced off the receiver's hands and deflected into the arms of Nohl Williams.
Allen has five touchdowns versus seven interceptions in his past five starts.
The Chiefs continue to face questions over whether they have padded their record with weaker opponents. Of their eight wins, only one - a season-opening victory against Denver - has come against an opponent with a winning record entering Week 12. Meantime, all three losses have come against winning teams.
The Bills, meanwhile, were coming off a four-game stretch in which they feasted in playing against backup and third-string quarterbacks.
Buffalo limited the NFL's best offense to 241 yards and contained Mahomes, who entered the outing combined for 13 TDs passing and averaging 309 yards over his past four games.
Buffalo did allow their first touchdown in four outings, dating to to Derrick Henry's two-yard run in a 36-10 win over Baltimore on November 1. They were also limited to a season-low 230 yards.

items.title: Mad about mara: the DIY dance movement helping young Nigerians escape the daily grind
items.summary:
As a student in the central Nigerian city of Ilorin, Lawal Habeeb Kola loved staying in his hostel room to produce beats rather than returning to his family house in Lagos, the more frenetic city of his birth.
In 2022, one of his beats became popular on TikTok, and a version featuring ad-libbed voca
items.text:
As a student in the central Nigerian city of Ilorin, Lawal Habeeb Kola loved staying in his hostel room to produce beats rather than returning to his family house in Lagos, the more frenetic city of his birth.
In 2022, one of his beats became popular on TikTok, and a version featuring ad-libbed vocals from a hypeman sent it viral. He was invited to the music video shoot in Lagos and thought his big break had finally come, but when the video was released, he was absent.
“I was in a restaurant and everybody was anticipating seeing me, but my face did not show once,” the 27-year old, known as DJ Khalipha, said. “I felt disgraced. I stopped posting the song.”
Khalipha retreated to his dorm and revisited the DIY “cruise beats” genre of dance music that he had previously worked in. Taking its name from the pidgin expression “catch cruise”, meaning to joke around, cruise beats is a lo-fi, frenetic genre that incorporates amusing voice samples from Nollywood and memes.
Khalipha raised the already fast 115-120 beats per minute of cruise beats to 140-150bpm, added melancholic undertones and named the new style mara, meaning to lose one’s senses. The popularity of the sound soared, eventually crossing over from the Lagos underground and becoming incorporated into the sound of mainstream musicians.
As the genre exploded, Khalipha lost creative control. “It became a trend that every producer and DJ was hopping on,” said Feranmi Abiola, 24, who directed the 2025 documentary Mara Mania. “They were making sounds and whether it was mara sound or not, they would just title it mara fever, mara this, mara that.”
Like its predecessors, mara’s spread was driven by choreography. One dancer, Obi “Odogwu Mara” Madubogwu, named himself after the sound and dropped dance routines on social media weekly, gaining street credibility. His death in unclear circumstances at the age of 26 galvanised interest in mara, especially among young Nigerians for whom posting and responding to dance challenges in his style became a form of escape from poor job prospects in Nigeria’s sluggish economy.
“We’ve seen area boys [street urchins] switching to become dancers,” said the producer Azzi On The Beat, an early adopter of mara who has stayed true to the sound. “The music is spiritual.”
The hectic but harmonious sound has become a fixture at raves, which in Nigeria take the form of street-style block-gatherings populated by young people tired of the markup on alcohol at nightclubs and “bottle culture” – the buying of expensive bottles of champagne and spirts in VIP sections, often as a means of flaunting wealth.
Top musicians have been enlisting the sound in search of new hits, but mara’s originators remain relatively unknown, their work often restricted to the thriving underground “TrenchTok” scene.
Khalipha said bookers assumed that mara DJs would have an air of chaos and violence, due to the raw sound of the music and its association with street culture.
Abiola agreed. “[Mara DJs] are not harmful, but they face stereotypes because of their background, how they look and how they dress,” she said. “In my documentary, I wanted people to see these people for who they were … young people innovating and contributing to the cultural identity of this generation. Regardless of where they are from, they deserve to be taken seriously.”
Without institutional backing, the DJs have been learning how to navigate the music industry on the go. When the samples they were using were flagged for copyright issues, they created their own instrumentals from scratch using plugins.
Many artists are self-funded, investing money earned as social media influencers or from royalties into shooting videos and promotion. Female dancers talk of sexual harassment and financial exploitation in the industry.
“The financial challenges are more apparent for the dancers, because people don’t really take dancers seriously,” said Abiola.
Pointing to a square littered with weeds and rubbish, where goats roamed next to a woman sieving black-eyed peas on a tray, Azzi’s 27-year-old manager, Sangokunle Anuoluwapo – known as Kadima – said: “We do most of our videos here.”
Despite the challenges, the people involved in mara harbour dreams of global traction. Support from the French embassy helped Azzi perform at festivals in Uganda and parts of Europe. A few industry friends on the rise or those who Kadima at one point managed also help intermittently with funding or promoting projects for free.
“I understand what we want for this culture so we keep pushing really hard,” said Kadima. “It’s family work, so we try to split revenues among everybody.”
Azzi was given a leg up from the Footprints of David Art Academy, a children’s dance theatre troupe that held performances behind his mother’s shop. He honed his dancing skills, learned how to drum, and met Kadima there. “We were taught how to fight through tough times,” Azzi said.
The art director Seun Awobajo launched the academy in 2005 with the aim of channelling the energy of disadvantaged children into creative endeavours. “[I had] the notion that no child is useless, they are only used less,” he said.
Awobajo is proud of his former wards and the mara scene more generally. “Being proud is an understatement,” he said. “But I think I feel more fulfilled seeing what they’ve become because these are children who the upper class of the society have written off.”

items.title: India’s Pant plays for New Zealand side under false name ‘Stan Stan’
items.summary:
India’s Pant plays for New Zealand side under false name ‘Stan Stan’
Rishabh Pant plays for Open House Swingers in New Zealand on eve of second Test as India wicketkeeper uses false name.
India’s star wicketkeeper-batsman Rishabh Pant used an unlikely forum to keep his eye sharp before the second Ne
items.text:
India’s Pant plays for New Zealand side under false name ‘Stan Stan’
Rishabh Pant plays for Open House Swingers in New Zealand on eve of second Test as India wicketkeeper uses false name.
India’s star wicketkeeper-batsman Rishabh Pant used an unlikely forum to keep his eye sharp before the second New Zealand Test – a social Last Man Stands match in Christchurch.
The 29-year-old, who plays for Lucknow Super Giants in the Indian Premier League, is one of the six most prolific hitters in Test history, hitting 108 across his 53 matches to sit second all time.
Six of those came in Wellington last week, where his 128 from 153 balls helped India set a record in New Zealand, 720-9 in the drawn match.
After a chance encounter in central Christchurch, Pant played Wednesday for the Open House Swingers in a Last Man Stands match against The Chosen Ones at Hagley Park – not to be confused with neighbouring Hagley Oval, where Pant will wear Indian whites this week.
Listed on the scorecard as Stan Stan, Pant blasted 54 from 21 balls to maintain his glittering form in New Zealand.
“I saw Rishabh going around on an electric bike,” Open House Swingers player Mohammad Safi told the New Zealand Herald.
“So I went and stopped him, and we start talking and taking a few photos and stuff, and I asked him, do you want to play cricket for us?
“He was like, OK, I’ll come and play for you guys. Then he came and padded up, went batting, and smashed a few sixes.”
Indian bowling coach Morne Morkel said he “nearly fell off my chair last night when I saw that”.
New Zealand captain Tom Latham said Pant’s midweek performance was “brilliant”.
“He’s obviously a real character of the game is Rishabh, so it’s great for him to give his experience back to the LMS teams.”
Safi told the New Zealand Herald the opposition did not recognise Pant while he wore his striking blue tracksuit.
Safi also said Pant used his cousin’s bat during the match.
“He was asking me to basically give him a single and stuff. Obviously, I was smashing longer sixes than him, and then he was like, give me a turn, let me show you how to hit it,” Safi said.
The Open House Swingers won the match by 16 runs, a feat Pant could not achieve in Wellington, as the Test ended in a draw.
India’s second Test against New Zealand begins Friday at Hagley Oval.
