items.title: Spain’s 2026 election explained in maps and charts
items.summary:
Spain’s 2026 election explained in maps and charts
Spaniards vote on November 29 in a snap general election. Here is how the system works, the parties and the key issues.
Spain will hold a snap election on November 29 that could bring the far right into government for the first time since the end of
items.text:
Spain’s 2026 election explained in maps and charts
Spaniards vote on November 29 in a snap general election. Here is how the system works, the parties and the key issues.
Spain will hold a snap election on November 29 that could bring the far right into government for the first time since the end of Francisco Franco’s dictatorship in 1975.
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez called the early vote last month after parliament rejected his government’s housing relief measures, which came during mass protests over rents and house prices.
Polls suggest the centre-right People’s Party (PP) will win most seats but will need the far-right Vox party to reach the 176 seats required for a majority in the 350-seat Congress of Deputies. Voters will also elect 208 members of the Senate.
About 38.7 million people aged 18 and above are eligible to vote, according to Spain’s National Statistics Institute (INE).
When will polls open?
Polling stations across Spain will be open on November 29 at 9am local time (08:00 GMT) and close at 8pm (19:00 GMT).
How does voting work?
Spain is a parliamentary monarchy. King Felipe VI is head of state, while the government is led by a prime minister who answers to the Cortes Generales, a parliament made up of two houses: the Congress of Deputies and the Senate.
The 350 members of the lower house, the Congress of Deputies, are elected in 52 constituencies by proportional representation. Rather than choosing individual candidates, voters pick a party, and each party puts forward a ranked list of candidates in every constituency.
Every province is guaranteed at least two seats and the autonomous cities of Ceuta and Melilla in North Africa get one each. The rest are distributed by population, which is why Madrid and Barcelona elect far more deputies than smaller provinces.
Within each constituency, seats are divided according to each party’s share of the vote and go to the candidates at the top of each list. A party needs at least 3 percent of the vote in a constituency to qualify for any seats there.
A party needs 176 of the 350 seats for a majority. If no party reaches that number, parties must form coalitions or strike deals to govern. After consulting party leaders, the king proposes a candidate for prime minister, who must then win an investiture vote in Congress.
Most members of the upper house, the Senate, are elected directly, with voters choosing individual candidates by name. In most provinces, each voter can back up to three candidates and the four with the most votes are elected. The remaining senators are appointed by Spain’s regional parliaments.
When will the results be announced?
Provisional results from the Interior Ministry will start coming in straight away, with the overall picture clear before midnight on Sunday.
In 2023, about 99 percent of votes had been counted by 11:45pm.
Spain’s current coalition government
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez leads a minority coalition government made up of the Spanish Socialist Workers’ Party (PSOE) and the left-wing Sumar alliance. The 22-member cabinet comprises Sanchez, three deputy prime ministers and 18 other ministers.
The three deputy prime ministers each oversee a major policy area: Carlos Cuerpo oversees the economy, Yolanda Diaz labour and the social economy and Sara Aagesen the ecological transition. Cuerpo is also acting transport minister after Oscar Puente resigned after last month’s train crash that killed 69 people.
Thirteen cabinet members belong to the PSOE and five to Sumar, while four are independents appointed by the PSOE.
Which are the main parties on the ballot?
- Socialist Party (PSOE), centre-left – Incumbent Pedro Sanchez is running again after more than eight years in office, which makes him Spain’s second-longest-serving prime minister since 1978, after Felipe Gonzalez. His final two years in power were overshadowed by corruption investigations involving his wife, his brother and former close allies.
- People’s Party (PP), centre-right – Alberto Nunez Feijoo, who has led the PP since 2022, is the party’s candidate. The PP won the most seats in the 2023 election but could not gather enough support to form a government.
- Vox, far right – Led by Santiago Abascal, who co-founded the party in 2014 after leaving the PP, Vox has become Spain’s third-largest party. It campaigns for tougher immigration rules, lower taxes and a hard line against Catalan and Basque separatism.
- Broad Front (Frente Amplio), left – Headed by Ada Colau, the former mayor of Barcelona, it is a new alliance that replaces Sumar, the left-wing grouping that has governed alongside Sanchez since 2023. Podemos, a former partner of Sumar, is running separately.
- Regional parties – Could again decide who governs. EH Bildu (Basque Country), the BNG (Galicia), the Basque Nationalist Party (PNV) and the left-wing Catalan pro-independence ERC have largely backed Sanchez. The centre-right Catalan pro-independence party Junts supported his 2023 investiture but has since repeatedly voted against his government.
What are the main issues?
According to a YouGov poll published on October 30 , the main issues according to the Spanish public are:
- Housing – Spain is short of 750,000 homes, according to the Bank of Spain, which warns that the gap could surpass one million by 2028. The average rent has reached 1,176 euros ($1,318) a month, almost exactly a young person’s average monthly salary of 1,191 euros ($1,334), according to the Spanish Youth Council. Anger over housing costs has fuelled nationwide protests.
- Immigration – Sanchez has been one of Europe’s leading advocates of migration and this year offered undocumented migrants a path to legal status, drawing almost 1.2 million applications. Vox, on the other hand, has pledged to deport all undocumented migrants, while the PP has promised tighter border controls in its manifesto.

items.text:
Israel uses south Lebanon Christian villages to try to divide and conquer
Israel is trying to fragment Lebanon by separating its Christian residents in south Lebanon from the rest.
Beirut, Lebanon – On Lebanon’s Independence Day on Sunday, Israel’s Arabic-language military spokesperson Ella Waweya posted a video on X in a classroom in Dibil, a Christian village in south Lebanon.
In the video, she wished Lebanese a happy national day, praised the singer Fairuz, and blamed the Lebanese armed group Hezbollah, which is fighting an ongoing war against Israel, for the hardships faced by the people in southern Lebanon.
The video drew widespread condemnation from Lebanese officials, including from Dibil’s municipality, who told local media that the visit took place around a month before the video was posted.
The council said the visit took place “without prior coordination with the school administration”. The Israeli military said an investigation was reviewing the incident and it is not clear whether Waweya had official approval to post the video.
Unlike neighbouring Shia Muslim villages, Christian villages in southern Lebanon have generally been allowed to stay on their lands during Israel’s war on Lebanon. But they still live under Israeli occupation.
“We’re in a giant prison,” Ayoub Khreish, the president of Ain Ebl municipality, told Al Jazeera from his village on Lebanon’s southern border. “We can only move around in these [neighbouring] villages. Anytime we want to go to Beirut, we need to get permission.”
This system goes through a so-called “mechanism”, whereby a request is submitted to the Lebanese Army, which passes it to the UN and then onto the Israelis for approval.
Now living under the Israeli military’s authority, these Christian villages are being used as part of an Israeli strategy to foment divides among the Lebanese population, experts told Al Jazeera.
Villages under the control of Israel
Israel launched a massive assault on Lebanon in October 2023, shortly after genocide in Gaza began, with approximately 9,000 people killed since then, according to Lebanon’s Ministry of Public Health.
Southern Lebanon, where Hezbollah has a presence, has been the area worst affected by the violence, with thousands of Israeli air raids and repeated Israeli raids in villages.
Israel’s war on Lebanon has left Christians in southern villages in a precarious position. Much of the south has been made uninhabitable by Israeli attacks and demolitions. While Shia Muslims have taken the overwhelming brunt of the violence, Christians have been killed in attacks and been displaced, too.
In early November, the mayors of five Christian villages appealed to the Council of Catholic Patriarchs and Bishops of Lebanon, asking for help so residents can remain on their land and displaced people can return.
“Help us make staying on our land a choice of life based on security, dignity, work and hope, rather than an anxious wait in uncertainty,” they wrote at the time.
Khreish, municipal president of Ain Ebl, said a little more than half of the town’s population fled since the start of the war. Daily convoys bring in food and other necessities, but the local economy has ground to a halt.
He initially hoped for a political solution to the crisis, but a June framework agreement between Israel and Lebanon that looked to have Israeli troops withdraw from the south and Hezbollah disarm has not progressed as originally hoped. Talks between the two sides have been stalled since August.
“We thought peace and a political solution would be closer than this,” he said. “But the opposite seems to be true; it’s far off.”
As the occupation drags on, Lebanese in these villages feel they are forced to deal with the political reality in front of them. Khreish said Israeli soldiers enter the village regularly and interact with locals.
“We’re no longer afraid of them,” Khreish said. “We’re under their authority, the authority of the Israeli military.”
Political weaponisation
Experts say this particular treatment of Christians in Lebanon is part of a wider strategy to fragment and divide the local population.
“It’s part of a longstanding strategy on behalf of Israel towards the minorities of the region to divide and conquer,” Munira Khayyat, author of Landscape of War: Ecologies of Resistance and Survival in South Lebanon, told Al Jazeera. “You see this happening, of course, in Palestine, and in Lebanon, they’ve always done this. They always had this strategy of separating the Christians from their social, ethnic, national and historical environment to reinvent them as foot soldiers for the Zionist cause.”
In July, Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who may soon be out of office, claimed that Lebanon’s Christians were asking Israel for protection from its Muslim neighbours.
“Christian villages in Lebanon, some of them have actually asked to be annexed to Israel, because we protect them against Hezbollah, Hezbollah fanatics who want to kill them, and we do the same things with Christians everywhere,” Netanyahu told Fox News.
Netanyahu’s claims were rejected by Lebanese officials, including Hanna al-Amil, president of the Rmeish Municipality, the largest Christian-majority border village.
A statement was signed by 15 villages in southern Lebanon that called the claim “completely fabricated” and “unrelated to reality”.
Michael Young, a Lebanese political analyst and writer at the Beirut-based Carnegie Center, said Israel aimed to show the outside world, and the US in particular, that it protects Christians and other minorities after its actions in Gaza turned public opinion heavily against it. In Gaza, Israel had bombed Christian churches, where many Palestinians sought refuge from the Israeli genocide.
“People like [US political commentator] Tucker Carlson are playing this up, so from a public relations perspective, they want to show they are friendly to all minorities; Druze, Christians and so on,” Young said.

items.text:
Major Thanksgiving storm brings flooding, flight delays across US
- Published
A massive Thanksgiving storm hammering the Midwest and north-east with heavy rain and winds, along with high tides out west, is causing widespread disruptions across the US.
More than 80 million Americans expected to be travelling this week. On Thursday 460 flights in the US were cancelled and another 2,508 flights into, out of, or within the US were delayed, tracking site FlightAware said.
The FAA has previously warned that delays would be possible "throughout the week" as a result of the rain and wind that are forecast.
Meanwhile, almost one million households were without power on Thursday night, with Pennsylvania, Maryland and Virginia the hardest hit states.
On Thursday, a powerful storm hit the eastern US, bringing damaging winds of up to 70mph, torrential rain, and major coastal flooding.
New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill declared a state of emergency as several communities along the Jersey Shore saw widespread flooding.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul also declared a state of emergency for New York City, Long Island and Westchester County.
In New York City, organisers of the annual Macy's Thanksgiving parade have postponed the event to Saturday.
Bridges closed in Maryland due to severe winds and waves battered beaches in Delaware as water seeped onto the boardwalk.
In Maryland, almost two million customers have been asked by the water utility to use water for essential use only due to "intermittent power disruptions".
On the wettest Thanksgiving on record in Washington DC, tidal waters surged and soaked runways at Reagan Washington National Airport, according to the National Water Prediction Service.
More than 980,000 households were reporting power outages by Thursday evening, with Pennsylvania, Virginia, Maryland and New Jersey hit particularly hard.
Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro said that utility providers were working tirelessly to restore power. Meanwhile, energy companies in Virginia and New Jersey warned it may take some time, even days, for power to return, as crews had to wait until it was safe to access damaged areas.
On Thursday afternoon, President Donald Trump said he would consider releasing emergency funds for the east coast as it faces down the holiday storm.
Across the US, severe weather is also descending on the West Coast. The NWS has warned of a series of Pacific storms that are expected to bring rain, mountain snow and strong winds.
Many are bracing for potential flooding as king tides peak along the coast.
Water levels along California's vast coastline could reach over 8ft (2.4 metres) in some areas on Thursday, according to the NWS, breaking records set just last month.
Both San Diego and Los Angeles reported a high tide of over 8ft earlier in the week, and beach-goers were advised to avoid coastal areas.
Train services along the Amtrak Pacific Surfliner, which runs along the California coastline, cancelled several trains due to "washout conditions from high tides", the company shared on social media.
Storms are also forecast for the Pacific Northwest, including the Canadian province of British Columbia.
In Miami, some travel delays persisted into Thursday after a FedEx plane overshot the runway the night before, which prompted the closure of all but one runway at the airport for a brief period.
A statement FedEx provided to US media confirmed that one of its flights had "experienced an issue upon landing".
It added: "We are grateful that our crew is safe and there are no reported injuries. We are coordinating closely with investigating authorities, and any additional questions should be referred to the FAA."
An airport employee who spoke anonymously to CBS News, the BBC's US partner, raised the possibility that rainy conditions had been a factor.
"They tried as hard as they could to stop, but I don't know if it was the weather because the rain and the wind were really bad, and they just couldn't stop in time and went right off the runway and veered off into the grass," they said.
Wednesday's incident in Miami came 11 weeks after a cargo plane crashed on landing at the same airport, killing five people and injuring five others in vehicles on the ground with which it collided.
The American Automobile Association (AAA) predicted that 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles (80km) from home for the Thanksgiving holiday over a seven-day period.
Rebecka Pieder contributed reporting.

items.text:
Thanksgiving storms leave nearly a million without power across the US
Severe weather across the US causes outages and flight delays as families and friends gather for the annual holiday.
Strong winds and heavy storms have knocked out power for nearly a million US homes and businesses and resulted in the rare postponement of Macy’s annual Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York City.
As Americans marked the annual holiday on Thursday, heavy storms disrupted travel across the country, with more than 2,000 flights to or from US destinations delayed and more than 400 cancelled, according to the flight tracking service FlightAware.
More than 900,000 homes and businesses were without electricity on Thursday evening, with the majority in East Coast states, according to the outage tracking website poweroutage.us. New Jersey and parts of New York were placed under a state of emergency.
The US National Weather Service issued wind advisories for northern Georgia, the majority of the mid-Atlantic and southern New England.
Two people were rescued from their cars in New York City due to flooding, according to Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
“There is no destination worth your safety,” Mamdani said. Similar rescues were reported in other coastal communities.
In Maryland, nearly two million water customers in Montgomery and Prince George’s counties were asked to conserve water because of intermittent power disruptions related to heavy rain. The storms also prompted several brief tornado warnings, including for a rare twister southeast of Seattle, Washington.
The Midwestern region witnessed heavy snowfall on Thursday, with some areas of Missouri recording up to 35cm of snow.
Meanwhile, waves driven by high tides caused flooding along the Pacific coast. The conditions were expected to continue into Friday, according to the National Weather Service.
Record tides along the California coast forced evacuations in areas from Humboldt County in the far north to southern Ventura County near Los Angeles.

items.text:
At least 13 Niger soldiers killed in Sanam armed attack
It remains unclear who carried out the attack on Niger’s National Guard in Tillaberi, near the Mali border.
At least 13 members of Niger’s National Guard have been killed and 20 wounded in an attack on their compound in Sanam, in the west of the country, the Defence Ministry has said.
In a statement read on state television, the ministry said the attack on Thursday was carried out by “numerous heavily armed assailants”, referring to the incident as a “terrorist attack”.
The ministry gave a provisional toll and said soldiers killed several attackers and destroyed their logistical infrastructure. Operations to track down the attackers are ongoing, it added.
The assault took place at about 5am local time (04:00 GMT), local and security sources told the Nigerien outlet ActuNiger.
Sanam is in the Tillaberi region, near the Mali border, where armed groups regularly attack security forces.
It was not clear who was behind the attack.
The attack comes two days after the ministry said 11 soldiers were killed in an attack attributed to Boko Haram in the Diffa region, in the southeast.
Violence across the border
In neighbouring Nigeria, suspected members of an armed group killed at least 30 people in villages in the central state of Niger on Tuesday.
They described it as retaliation for the killing of many Fulani herders days earlier.
In Nigeria’s northeast, President Bola Tinubu promised on Wednesday to restore peace to a region hit by a rebellion led by Boko Haram and the ISIL (ISIS) affiliate in West Africa Province, as he campaigns for re-election.

items.text:
Trump downplays Russia, China support for Iran during talks with US troops
Trump praises US troops for their role in the war on Iran and says he has spoken to Netanyahu in recent days.
United States President Donald Trump has claimed Iran possesses missiles capable of reaching Europe and downplayed Russia and China’s support for Tehran while speaking to US military personnel by phone for the Thanksgiving holiday.
Taking questions from reporters at his Mar-a-Lago residence in Florida on Thursday, Trump said without “peace in the Middle East”, Iran could launch nuclear attacks against Israel and other countries in the region.
“We don’t need Middle East oil. But what we do need is we need peace in the Middle East,” Trump said, as OPEC ministers are scheduled to meet on Sunday to weigh 2027 oil production targets.
The US president and First Lady Melania Trump called US service members deployed across the region to praise their role in the war on Iran, including personnel at the al-Dhafra airbase in the United Arab Emirates and the Prince Sultan airbase in Saudi Arabia.
“Each of you is playing an essential role to protect not only our country today but future generations of Americans by ensuring that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon,” he said.
When asked if the US would renew strikes on Iran, the president said: “If we do something, we will definitely hit Pickaxe Mountain.” Trump also told reporters he spoke with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in recent days.
The US is still offering Iran an opening to negotiate, according to Trump, who said: “We’re trying to be nice. We’re giving them every chance to make a deal and save a lot of lives, but I’m not sure if they are gonna take advantage of that.”
He downplayed the importance of intelligence-sharing by Russia and China with Iran, amid reports that the two countries helped Tehran target US bases.
“My meeting with President Xi was an incredible meeting. I think that they’re very little involved with Iran. They could get involved, but involvement to me would mean shooting, not giving them little information,” Trump said during the short news conference.
“We do the same thing, by the way. And you know, when they say that they may be spying on us, well, we spy on them too,” he added.
Trump’s statements come as Iran steps up attacks on US military targets across the region. On Saturday, Bahrain reported an Iranian attack on a civilian industrial facility while Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed it targeted US air defence radars in the country.
Kuwait said on Thursday that an Iranian drone attack on a “vital site” killed two Italian workers and injured four others. Tehran has denied involvement in the attack.
Trump told deployed service members, “You’re going to continue that deployment, and we have victory at hand,” referring to the war on Iran.
“It’s [victory] going to be whenever I want it to be, to be honest,” he added.

Japan’s benchmark Nikkei 225 on Friday added 0.7 percent to 57,919.30 in morning trading. Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 rose 0.4 percent to 8,800.50. South Korea’s Kospi surged 2.2 percent to 4,812.65.
Hong Kong’s Hang Seng edged up 0.4 percent to 22,310.11.
Stocks in Indonesia, Singapore and the Philippines also rose, while New Zealand’s bourse edged down as Prime Minister Christopher Luxon’s right-wing coalition lost its parliamentary majority, plunging the country into political uncertainty with a centrist party set to play a decisive role in forming the next government.
Buying of stocks tied to artificial intelligence (AI) has been pushing benchmarks higher, despite some profit-taking that has kept those gains in check.
In Japan, Tokyo Electron and Advantest Corp stocks dropped in morning trading but quickly recovered their losses, underlining the continuing appeal of stocks in the semiconductor and AI sectors.
With Wall Street closed for the Thanksgiving holiday on Thursday, traders had no new business-driving catalysts heading into the weekend, though they remain on edge over concerns about the AI boom.
They were also keeping an eye on possible retaliation against US President Donald Trump’s proposed tariffs of up to 20 percent on some of the United States’ biggest trading partners, including China, the European Union, India, Japan and South Korea.
Also in view is the Federal Reserve’s next interest rate decision next month, with speculation swirling that it could opt for a hefty 50-basis-point increase instead of the usual 25 points.
Oil prices extended Thursday’s gains of more than 1 percent amid fresh concerns over an escalation of hostilities in the Middle East after Iran-aligned Houthis struck a Saudi refinery, temporarily halting some operations. That came after an attack on another hub in the Gulf earlier in the week.
In company news, Japan Tobacco rallied more than 4 percent following a report that it was considering joining up with US giant Altria for a takeover of Britain’s Imperial Brands. Imperial jumped 13 percent in London on Thursday.
Japan Tobacco is dealing with an $8.9bn hit after the Russian government seized all seven of its local subsidiaries, as relations with Tokyo worsen following the arrest of a Japanese journalist on spying allegations.

New Zealand election ends in hung parliament

The final vote in New Zealand's election showed on Friday that neither the ruling conservatives nor the opposition bloc has enough seats to form a majority government.
The incumbent three-way coalition government is led by Prime Minister
items.text:
New Zealand election ends in hung parliament
November 27, 2026
The final vote in New Zealand's election showed on Friday that neither the ruling conservatives nor the opposition bloc has enough seats to form a majority government.
The incumbent three-way coalition government is led by Prime Minister Christopher Luxon of the center-right National Party.
He governed with two other smaller right parties. The incumbent coalition government won 65 seats, two down from election night, final results show.
The left-wing opposition bloc, led by the Labour Party's Chris Hipkins, won 58 seats, up by one from election night.
In terms of vote share of each of the main parties, Luxon's center-right National Party secured 40 seats, while Hipkins main center-left Labour Party won 36 seats.
The official vote count was released after election authorities counted 400,000 so-called special votes.
Those include ballots cast by New Zealanders living abroad.
Opportunity Party to play kingmaker role in formation of next government
Preliminary results from the November 7 election showed that the ruling coalition held a slim, two-seat majority — that's now been adjusted to the coalition falling short of a majority by a single seat.
The figures leave a new entrant to parliament, the Opportunity Party, as having a preeminent position because it will decide the shape of the next government.
The leader of the centrist party, Qiulae Wong, a 38-year-old former business consultant and a political newcomer, has said earlier this month that she was willing to speak with either party to form a government.
Luxon says negotiations with Opportunity Party will take time
Luxon will have to negotiate with the Opportunity Party if he wants to form the next government.
He said those negotiations will be "challenging" and will take time.
"I want to be upfront with New Zealanders. These negotiations may be challenging, and they could take some time," he told journalists.
"But getting it right matters far more than getting it done quickly. New Zealanders need a government that is stable, that works together, and will last for the full term," he added.
Experts say that if Luxon is not able to form a government with Opportunity, then New Zealanders will have to return to the polls for a new election, according to Australia's public broadcaster.

It now needs the support of the centrist O
items.text:
New Zealand's ruling coalition falls short of parliamentary majority by one seat
- Published
New Zealand's ruling coalition has fallen short of a parliamentary majority by one seat, following a campaign shaped by a sluggish economy and disillusioned voters.
It now needs the support of the centrist Opportunity Party to remain in power. If they cannot reach a deal, the country may have to go back to the polls.
The incumbent National Party led by Prime Minister Christopher Luxon secured 40 out of 130 seats, while its coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First took 13 and 12 respectively.
A government led by the centre-left Labour Party is not possible, official results on Friday show, as the bloc would not have enough seats even if Opportunity threw its weight behind it.
Luxon on Friday acknowledged that negotiations "may be challenging" and will take some time.
"Kiwis won't thank us for rushing to an agreement that falls apart or for sending them back to the polls," he told reporters.
Labour secured 36 seats, The Greens took 17, while Te Pāti Māori, which represents Māori interests, picked up five.
Opportunity, which has been described as this election's kingmaker, secured seven seats. Opportunity's leader Qiulae Wong told reporters her party will negotiate with National, but that all options remain on the table.
"There are seven parties in parliment and everyone is responsible for making sure we do everything we can to deliver a stable government for New Zealand. It's not just up to us," she said on Friday.
Preliminary results on 7 November, election day, had projected that National combined with its coalition partners would have a slim lead over the left-leaning bloc.
But today's official tally shows it had lost two seats on special votes - cast by citizens who were overseas or outside of their registered electorate on election day - which typically skew left.
Some of National's key election pledges include lower taxes, cheaper energy, more renewable generation, and a greater focus on defence.
Labour, meanwhile, had campaigned to cut healthcare, public transport and fuel costs, more government support for social housing, among other things.
New Zealand's mixed-member proportional voting system means most governments are coalitions. Each voter makes two choices – for the representative of their constituency in parliament and a political party.
In earlier interviews with the BBC, many voters had expressed frustration over spiralling costs of living and high unemployment across the country, with declining faith in their political leadership.
"There's this kind of apathy and a bit of dread," said 21-year-old Imogen Vlutger.
A 40-year-old man said he didn't vote as he could not bring himself to tick any of the boxes on the ballot paper.
More than half of the country no longer see New Zealand as a land of opportunity, according to a survey by the Helen Clark Foundation, a public policy think tank.
Kiwis have been leaving the country in record numbers, with many of them, including former prime minister Jacinda Arden, moving to Australia.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Ukraine has information that Russia is preparing a new mass s
items.text:
Zelenskyy warns of major Russian attack as Trump urges Putin to ‘pull back’
Trump says he urged Putin to ‘pull back’ military aggression in Europe amid escalating Russian and Ukrainian attacks.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Ukraine has information that Russia is preparing a new mass strike on the country in the coming days.
“Unfortunately, we have information about a new mass strike being prepared by the Russians,” he said in his nightly video address on Thursday. “In the coming days, please pay attention to the alarms of missile threats.”
It was the second such warning from Zelenskyy this week. He also had a message for Moscow: “We will rebuild what is ours and retaliate against every Russian strike.”
Trump urges Putin to pull back
US President Donald Trump said he had pressed Russian President Vladimir Putin to ease Russia’s military actions in Europe.
In a post on Truth Social, Trump said he spent “a lot of time” in talks with Putin in China on the issue of Putin pulling back “all Military aggression against territories throughout Europe”.
“Thousands of people are being killed each and every month, A COMPLETE BLOODBATH,” Trump wrote. He said he hoped that would allow a deal between Russia and Ukraine to be “made quickly”, which he called “a strong possibility”.
Trump said he updated NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte on the talks during a meeting at his Mar-a-Lago club in Florida on Wednesday night.
Latest attacks
Russia struck Kyiv with ballistic missiles overnight, wounding seven people and hitting a shopping centre and two other buildings, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
Moscow said it hit drone-related sites in the city. Russian forces have attacked Kyiv and other cities almost continuously since September.
Ukraine said its drones hit an oil refinery in Russia’s southern Krasnodar region, oil reservoirs at a Transneft facility in Bashkortostan and the Marinovka military airfield in the Volgograd region.
Ukraine has also widened its attacks at sea. On Monday, Zelenskyy said Ukraine used seven naval drones to hit the Russian corvette Merkury and the cargo ship Angara off Libya. Libyan officials told the Associated Press news agency that the Merkury was heavily damaged but not sunk.
At about the same time, a suspected Ukrainian drone struck the Russia-bound cargo ship Sparta II in the Baltic Sea, near Finland. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov called the attacks a “very dangerous trend“.
At least four Russian vessels have been targeted this month.
Europe’s funding for Ukraine
European Union leaders are struggling at a summit in Brussels to agree on a new 45 billion euro ($49bn) loan to help Ukraine meet its economic and military needs next year. It would come on top of a 90 billion euro ($99bn) loan, agreed nearly a year ago, that covers most of Ukraine’s government needs for 2026 and 2027.
Early on Friday in Brussels, European Council President Antonio Costa said that 24 member states supported the new loan, as talks on the bloc’s next seven-year budget stretched on.
The loan is tangled up with the EU’s budget for 2028 to 2034, which includes about $110bn for Ukraine over seven years. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has threatened to hold up the budget unless all member states make a “collective commitment” to Ukraine.
North Korea ‘pauses’ arms deliveries
Ukraine’s military intelligence agency (GUR) said on Thursday that North Korea has temporarily halted some military cooperation with Russia after diplomatic tensions between the allies.
It said this includes deliveries of KN-23 ballistic missiles and artillery shells, and Russian military flights over North Korean territory.
GUR said North Korea’s Foreign Minister Choe Son-hui announced the pause last month in response to a Russian deputy foreign minister’s assertion that Moscow would help ease tensions between Seoul and Pyongyang.
GUR also said Pyongyang is holding off on a Russian request to raise North Korea’s military presence in Russia from about 8,500 to 50,000 troops.
It added that North Korean units remain in Russia’s Kursk region and that a North Korean missile unit has been in the Voronezh region since mid-summer, from where Russia strikes Ukraine.
South Korean and Western intelligence agencies have said Pyongyang sent more than 10,000 soldiers to Russia’s Kursk region in 2024, along with artillery shells, missiles and long-range rocket systems.
Strikes continue
On November 20, Russia fired more than 400 drones and 110 missiles at Ukraine, killing eight people, Zelenskyy said.
It was one of the largest attacks of the war and followed Putin’s vow to retaliate for Ukrainian strikes on the Kerch Bridge linking Russia to Crimea.

items.title: Hard Drive pricing has gotten bad
items.summary: For years now, I’ve made it an annual tradition to replace one or two hard drives on Black Friday. I typically run around ten physical disks, and swapping a couple out each year means I almost never have a drive older than five years in my systems. I’ve even previously made videos about shucking dis
items.text:
For years now, I’ve made it an annual tradition to replace one or two hard drives on Black Friday. I typically run around ten physical disks, and swapping a couple out each year means I almost never have a drive older than five years in my systems. I’ve even previously made videos about shucking disks around this time of year.
But current hardware pricing is totally screwed. So what is a lifelong self-hoster to do in times like these? With disk capacities increasing massively over the last 10 years I can now fit 20TB per slot. This means I could realistically go from ten spinners to five, and not really feel it too acutely. This will mean redoing my zpool layouts, which in turn means shuffling some data around as ZFS doesn’t like changes to the layout of existing pools. But, at these prices, I’m starting to think the hassle might be worth it.
Let’s take a look at disk prices over the past 8 years in today’s post.
The 20TB WD EasyStore I bought for $249.99 in November 2024 is, today, on sale, $549.99 this Black Friday. $300 more than 2 years ago for the same product, from the same store. It shows just how bad hard drive pricing has gotten (BestBuy 20TB listing).
Shucking is homelab speak for taking a perfectly good external drive out of its USB enclosure and sticking the SATA drive in your server. At $12.50/TB it was a fantastically affordable way to get massive amounts of storage. At $27.50/TB, absolutely not.
I dug through my receipts
In November 2018 I bought five 10TB EasyStores for $179.99 each. At the time I wrote about doing the rounds of my local Best Buys to pickup more drives on Black Friday as quantities were limited at each location (My 2018 server build log).
October 2023 was my best haul on a per-TB basis. Three 18TB drives put 54TB in my hands for $599.97. This year’s “deal” is fifty bucks shy of that entire order. Best Buy was still advertising those 18TB drives for $199.99 in November 2023. November 2023 deal archive
What about ServerPartDeals?
Buying refurbished or recertified enterprise drives used to be an easy way to bring the cost down. In August 2024 I bought four recertified 14TB Ultrastars from ServerPartDeals for $529.96 before tax. That was 56TB at $9.46/TB, even cheaper than the EasyStores and no shucking to do.
The sad truth is that across the board prices are up a minimum of 58%, and sometimes as much as 218% in just a year or two.
How we got down to three HDD makers
When the EasyStore is that bad, my first instinct is to shop around. Maybe I should try another retailer (to be clear I’m not blaming BestBuy for any of this), buy an enterprise drive, see what’s available recertified. But follow those listings back to the companies that actually make the drives and the choices narrow pretty quickly. There are three big HDD makers left. How did we end up with so few?
Maxtor bought Quantum’s hard drive business in 2001, then Seagate bought Maxtor in 2006. Hitachi combined IBM’s disk business with its own to form HGST in 2003, and Toshiba bought Fujitsu’s HDD business in 2009. Seagate bought Samsung’s HDD business in December 2011, and Western Digital bought HGST in March 2012. The FTC required WD to sell desktop-drive manufacturing assets to Toshiba to keep a third supplier in that market. That left Seagate, Western Digital and Toshiba.
The 2011 Thailand floods hit while those last two deals were underway. WD halted production at all its Thai plants, and its average hard drive selling price went from $45 in fiscal 2011 to $62 in fiscal 2012. There was also a price-fixing case further up the supply chain. NHK Spring pleaded guilty in 2019 to fixing prices for the suspension assemblies that hold the read/write heads, and the court approved a $28.5 million fine. WD’s 2012 annual report · Ninth Circuit opinion
Market collusion and cartel pricing
It’s hard to have anything positive to say in this post. The HDD manufacturing market is so consolidated nowadays - just like the memory market which is equally screwed - that it’s hard to see this as anything but mass market collusion by the HDD manufacturing cartel.
Three companies is an awfully short list when you need to buy a hard drive. And with 89% of WD’s revenue coming from its cloud business in fiscal 2026, I don’t reckon those of us buying a couple of drives for a home server have much impact here. Just like with Nvidia and Micron, consumer markets just aren’t valuable enough so we have to make do with the crumbs instead.
As of November 26, 2026, the 20TB is 2.2× what I paid for the exact same SKU in 2024. It’s also $270 more than I paid for it in May 2025. And if you’re thinking you’ll just buy a smaller one, Best Buy’s 8TB Black Friday special is $299.99. That’s $37.50/TB and fifty bucks more than my 20TB cost two years ago. Best Buy’s EasyStore listings
The jump gets sillier when you price a whole NAS. Four of those 20TB drives would have been $999.96 at my 2024 price. This week they’d be $2,199.96. That’s another $1,200 before you’ve bought a case, a board or a single stick of RAM. And the price per usable terabyte only gets worse once you set aside a drive for parity.
If I can wish for one thing in 2027, it would be for hardware pricing to return to reasonable levels. I fear it may take a lot longer than that, though. So making do with less is going to be the new normal for a while. And in that creative constraint, maybe we’ll have some fun along the way instead.

Th
items.text:
Global news agency AFP reports cyberattack, shuts down content platform
France’s cybersecurity chief urges collective action to combat unprecedented threat levels in the nation.
Agence France-Presse (AFP) has been hit by a cyberattack, requiring the AFP Forum content platform to be taken offline.
The France-based international news agency’s management said on Thursday that it is currently investigating the circumstances of the cyberattack, including who was behind it.
“AFP was hit by a cyber attack overnight, starting at 1:30 am (Paris time) [00:30 GMT]. The target was AFP Forum, one of the platforms our clients use to browse and download our content,” an internal email from AFP management said.
“As soon as the intrusion was detected, our teams moved immediately to contain the intrusion and took AFP Forum offline as a precautionary measure. AFP Forum remains unavailable until further notice.”
AFP is reportedly offering backup solutions to the agency’s subscribers while the portal is offline.
France’s cybersecurity chief, Vincent Strubel, warned on Thursday that the country faces an unprecedented level of cybersecurity threats and called for collective efforts to strengthen defences against attacks.
“We are facing a level of threat that is unprecedented, with an intensity we have never experienced before,” Strubel said in an interview with France Inter radio.
The incident is the latest in a slew of cybersecurity disruptions across European countries. FIFA, which is based in Zurich, Switzerland, confirmed to Al Jazeera on Thursday that it had been the victim of a cyberattack that gave unauthorised access to personal and business information.
In October, several French supermarkets were hit by an “unprecedented” cyberattack that raised the temperature of fridges and freezers to as high as 50 degrees Celsius (122F).
Temperature spikes were also recorded in stores in 10 other European countries in early November, including the United Kingdom, Germany, Belgium and Sweden.
France accused Tehran of being behind the October attack and summoned Iran’s ambassador to Paris to “lodge a very strong protest”.
Iran called Paris’s accusations “baseless” and condemned the “hackneyed policy of levelling accusations against the Islamic republic”.

items.summary:
Met Police ruined my life, says Kenyan man wrongly convicted over attack on UK couple
- Published
A Kenyan woodcutter who was wrongly convicted and sentenced to death over an attack on a British couple has told the BBC that actions by London's Metropolitan Police involved in the case destroyed his l
items.text:
Met Police ruined my life, says Kenyan man wrongly convicted over attack on UK couple
- Published
A Kenyan woodcutter who was wrongly convicted and sentenced to death over an attack on a British couple has told the BBC that actions by London's Metropolitan Police involved in the case destroyed his life.
Somali gunmen broke into David and Judith Tebbutt's beach bungalow on the Kenyan coast in 2011. They shot David dead and abducted Judith, holding her captive in Somalia for six months.
Met detectives flew to Kenya to assist the investigation. Their evidence helped convict Ali Kololo, who spent more than a decade in prison before his conviction was overturned.
Kololo is suing the Met, claiming a senior officer, former Detective Superintendent Neil Hibberd, gave misleading evidence at his trial and acted unlawfully to secure his conviction.
In his first media interview, he told the BBC about his 15-year ordeal and his fight for compensation, which the Met is challenging in court.
We meet on Lamu, a small island off Kenya's northern coast, once a thriving Swahili port. People and goods are still carted through its narrow stone streets by donkey rather than car.
It was here, in 2013, that Kololo was sentenced to death.
Standing at the jetty, where police once brought him ashore in handcuffs, he relishes being free. But he is struggling to rebuild his life.
"Everything was taken from me. I'm starting from zero. I don't think I'll ever go back to who I was before," he says.
Before his arrest, Kololo lived with his wife and their three young children. He had once worked as a groundskeeper at the resort where the Tebbutts were staying, but by 2011 he earned his living felling trees in a local forest and selling the wood.
"My life was very good," he says. "I was fending for myself, taking good care of my family."
Within 24 hours of the attack, Kenyan police had arrested him.
"I was beaten with clubs and thrown into a car," he says. "They beat me for days, burning me with cigarettes, forcing me to confess to things. They subjected me to torture like no other."
Kololo could not read or write. He says police made him put his thumbprint on a statement claiming he had led the attackers to the Tebbutts.
"I didn't understand anything," he says, calling the statement "a mountain of lies". "I signed it without knowing what it was because of the state they had put me in".
The Kenyan police told us it "at all times strives to work within the law". Kololo is not suing them.
Within days of the attack, a team of Met officers, led by then Detective Superintendent Neil Hibberd, arrived to support the Kenyan investigation. The UK government had instructed the officers not to accept information from the Kenyan authorities that had been obtained by interrogating detainees.
But Hibberd requested Kololo's statement and later relied on it when giving evidence for the prosecution at his trial.
In court, Hibberd also presented evidence linking Kololo to the attack. He told the Kenyan court Kololo had been wearing a type of shoe that matched footwear marks found in the sand at the resort.
The officer who had arrested Kololo said he was barefoot when he was handed to police. Hibberd did not disclose that the Met's own forensic examination could not establish whether the shoe in question had made the marks.
At the trial, Kololo did not initially have a lawyer. He had to cross-examine all the prosecution witnesses himself, including Hibberd, through an interpreter who spoke Swahili, which was not Kololo's first language.
"I believe I was framed because I am a poor man and I did not have the strength or means to fight for myself," Kololo says.
Kololo was convicted of kidnap and robbery with violence - the only person ever convicted in connection with the attack. He spent three years on death row before his sentence was commuted to life imprisonment.
He recalls seeing his prison file. In the space for the expiry date, someone had written "death".
"I was completely heartbroken. I believed I could be executed at any moment, and I would never see my family, my children, ever again."
Years later, the UK's Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) established that Hibberd had omitted significant forensic evidence at the trial. It found that he would have had a case to answer for gross misconduct, but he could not face disciplinary proceedings because he had retired from the force. At the time, his lawyer said Hibberd absolutely disagreed with the report's findings.
In April 2023, Kenya's High Court quashed Kololo's conviction, because of doubts over the prosecution's evidence. This followed years of work by the legal charity Reprieve and a Kenyan lawyer, Alfred Olaba, who represented him for free.
They were supported by Judith Tebbutt, who believed Kololo was innocent. In an interview with the BBC in 2022, she said he had been scapegoated by Scotland Yard.
"He was not there on the night. He was not part of the group that held me. They've put this man in prison without any real evidence."
More than three years after his release, Kololo says he is still living with the effects of his torture and decade in prison. As we walk the narrow streets of Lamu's old town, his thin frame moves stiffly. He is on edge. "My mind is not good," he says. "I have not recovered."
He remembers being kept in a filthy, bedbug-ridden cell with up to eight other inmates, which he thought he would never leave. Twice he contracted tuberculosis and nearly died.
Kololo is now too frail to do the woodcutting he once relied on to make a living. He tries to grow enough to eat on the land around his home, but erratic rain makes it difficult.
"I have nothing. On the days I get food, I eat, and on the days I don't, I endure."
He lives alone in a mud hut. His wife divorced him after he went to prison, and their children went to live with his mother. They dropped out of school because the family could not pay the fees. Kololo says they were not allowed to visit him

'Priceless' Duran proves 'the man' but is he papering over cracks at Celtic?

items.text:
'Priceless' Duran proves 'the man' but is he papering over cracks at Celtic?
- Published
"Duran is priceless for us at the moment".
It would be difficult for a football manager to muster up a higher compliment for one of his players - given he should know exactly how much he did cost - but Celtic boss Martin O'Neill was rightly effusive in his praise for Camilo Duran.
With 15 goals in 23 appearances, six assists, and another late European winner on Thursday, the Colombian was once again the main man for a struggling Celtic side.
His double against Besiktas breathed life into their Europa League campaign last time out, and his late leap to nod in the winner against Torreense kept it alive.
Duran, 24, started on the bench but was brought on with just over half an hour to go as O'Neill watched his side labour against a team currently 13th in the Portuguese second tier.
Celtic would still be searching for their first European win were it not for their summer arrival from Qarabag, whose goals have played a key part in keeping his team within touching distance of a play-off spot with three fixtures to play.
"He's taken on this mantle of being the man and he's been fantastic," said O'Neill, who started Duran on the bench. "We tried a similar approach against Besiktas.
"Sometimes by the time Duran gets subbed on, you could be behind. But I think that's the sign of a brilliant player, he'll do something.
"He's not a big guy but he's just a super footballer, a super, super footballer."
Papering over cracks or quality in depth?
Duran's summer arrival was overshadowed when, just over a fortnight later, a club-record fee was paid to Bodo Glimt for another striker, Kasper Hogh.
While recent weeks have been dominated by debates over Duran or Hogh, the debate now seems settled, with the Colombian operating on a different level from his striking counterpart.
Anyone watching Celtic in Portugal would have watched Hogh find space a handful of times in the area, but repeatedly fail to find a team-mate or trouble the goalkeeper. Duran didn't need to be asked twice.
"I don't know how many touches he got, but he had the telling touch," James McFadden said on Sportsound post-match.
Duran's goals have also proved decisive in securing domestic points against Falkirk and Hibernian, and with Celtic just a point clear of Rangers, he is indeed invaluable.
Despite his late header giving the thousands of travelling Celtic fans a thrilling end to a relatively turgid game, the intervention is another significant moment in a season that is threatening to unravel if individual performances fail to continue papering over glaring deficiencies across the park.
If the lively Jota - who lasted 74 minutes - was not creating chances, tormenting full-backs or digging out enticing crosses in the first half, Celtic seemed without any real plan of attack.
Yang and Luke McCowan's involvements were limited at best, Hogh's chance to stake a claim was sub-par to be kind, and there was no driving force from the middle of the park to show some impetus.
Arithmetically, Celtic can still finish in any position in the Europa League table. But if they are to claim a playoff or automatic qualification spot, they will need Duran to remain in such a rich vein of form.
What are the fans saying?
Brian: Embarrassed by that performance, I know that there no easy games in Europe, couldn't pass the ball, not fit enough, no style of play and poorly coached. The club is in decline.
John: Celtic are just an average side these days - there should be no expectation.
Ted: That was just embarrassing. The 31st team in Portugal made us look ordinary. Go now Martin with dignity intact and preserve your achievements. Thus mob will drag you down.
Allan: Outclassed and out paced by Torreense, Celtic played poorly with a lot of comedy of errors in their play. But Yippee hee, Celtic. Won with a late goal from Duran.
Liam: This can't go on any further now, regardless of the result. MON is done and the coaching staff are done. Booing substitutions is the end, never mind a performance like this against second division opposition. The board can resign too.
Alec: Total embarrassment. Barring Jota, there was a complete lack of creativity, quality, urgency and belief. Time for the board to make the right decisions, get a new manager in and get rid of at least 10 of those players on show tonight.

items.title: Argentina bars Central Bank from printing money to fund government spending
items.summary:
Argentina bars Central Bank from printing money to fund government spending
The South American country’s Senate also advanced a proposal to suspend primary elections ahead of the 2027 presidential race.
Argentina’s legislature has pushed forward a series of bills that would implement changes sought
items.text:
Argentina bars Central Bank from printing money to fund government spending
The South American country’s Senate also advanced a proposal to suspend primary elections ahead of the 2027 presidential race.
Argentina’s legislature has pushed forward a series of bills that would implement changes sought by President Javier Milei, including barring the Central Bank from printing extra money for government expenses.
On Thursday, the Argentinian Chamber of Deputies gave final approval to a bill imposing restrictions on the Central Bank, defining its “primary and fundamental mission” as maintaining the value of the country’s currency.
Under past administrations, the Central Bank has printed additional funds to help cover government expenses, contributing to the country’s once sky-high inflation, which reached more than 200 percent in 2023.
Milei, a libertarian economist, swept into office that year on a promise to tame runaway inflation and slash government spending.
Under his leadership, inflation has declined, though poverty has surged. Economists also believe Argentina may be drifting into a recession, with economic activity diminished in recent months.
Still, Milei’s office celebrated the Senate’s passage of the Central Bank bill with a presidential statement.
“This marks the end of nearly two decades of political manipulation at the Central Bank,” the statement said.
The bank, founded in 1935, had experienced “91 years of plunder, expropriation, impunity, and institutional decay” up to this point, it added.
The vote in the Chamber of Deputies was 141 to zero, with 99 abstentions.
The Senate previously passed the bill, though it removed language Milei had pressed for, which would have required a two-thirds vote in both chambers of Congress to remove Central Bank governors.
Bill seeks to suspend primary elections
Also on Thursday, Argentina’s Senate advanced a bill to reform the country’s elections by suspending its primaries.
Unlike the Central Bank reform, that bill was not final. It still needs to pass the Chamber of Deputies.
The bill, however, comes less than a year before Argentina is slated to hold its next presidential election. Milei is expected to seek re-election in the October 24 vote.
Critics see the suspension of primaries as a means for Milei to avoid early pushback in his campaign.
A dismal primary result, they say, could weaken his momentum ahead of the general election and cause unfavourable economic fluctuations. Milei has long faced public discontent over his programme of economic austerity.
Thursday’s bill would also reduce public financing for political parties and eliminate a mandatory presidential debate ahead of general elections.
Senators approved the legislation by a vote of 43 to 29. While members of Milei’s La Libertad Avanza party touted the bill as a means of simplifying Argentina’s elections, opponents warned it could erode democratic norms.
“Milei now wants to change the rules of democracy to improve his chances of reelection by cheating,” Buenos Aires province Governor Axel Kicillof, a potential challenger to Milei, said in a social media post.

Nottingham Forest’s last couple of seasons have been a story of good runs and bad runs, but it may help to know that last season’s encounters with Chelsea both presaged changes of fortune. After they lost to Chelsea in October, a seventh defeat in 10 winless games, Forest’s form improved and they won seven of their next 12 in all competitions. But after beating Chelsea in May, their seventh victory in a 10-game unbeaten run, Forest’s form dipped dramatically and they have won only twice since. Oliver Glasner’s criticism of players whose “standards [are] not high enough” is clearly designed to raise them. Time will tell if it has worked but the key man this week is one who should have no issues with motivation and whose English is at least decent. Liam Delap, facing the side that signed and swiftly discarded him, could really trouble Wesley Fofana and Levi Colwill. The Chelsea centre-back pairing were described as playing like “two novices” by Jamie Carragher after they were outfought by Dominic Calvert-Lewin last week. “Until they sign that dominant centre-back and leader, they’ve got absolutely no chance of achieving anything,” Carragher concluded. Simon Burnton
Nottingham Forest v Chelsea, Friday 8pm (all times GMT)
When Leeds recruited Dominic Calvert-Lewin on a free transfer during the summer of 2025 it is fair to say many of their fans were underwhelmed. Now though the news that the England centre-forward has penned a contract extension at Elland Road is a cause for celebration in West Yorkshire. Calvert-Lewin had proved somewhat injury-prone at his former club, Everton, yet Daniel Farke evidently knew what he was doing. The newly robust 29-year-old has scored 18 goals in 46 Premier League appearances for Leeds, 17 arriving in the last 36 games. With Calvert-Lewin now having signed a new, improved deal extending until 2029, attention is turning to Farke’s own contract. The German’s current agreement expires next summer but renewal talks have been under way for some time and, for the moment at least, the normally open Leeds manager has turned coy. “I’ve fallen in love with the club,” said Farke ahead of his upwardly mobile team’s home meeting with Coventry. “But I’m not willing to speak about my future.” Louise Taylor
Leeds v Coventry, Saturday 3pm
Mauricio Pochettino will send out his first Manchester United XI at Old Trafford on Saturday hoping Senne Lammens’ errors for the season are over. The fumble of a simple aerial ball late on at Sporting that allowed Luis Suárez to salvage a point on Wednesday was dismal from the goalkeeper despite his head coach’s protestations that the backline as a collective was at fault for allowing the opening. Karl Darlow, United’s second choice, has Premier League experience after a stint as Leeds’ first choice towards the end of last season but has played only 30 games in all divisions in the past three years. That means, probably, that Pochettino will retain Lammens but if more mistakes follow then the Wales international Darlow may be handed his chance. Jamie Jackson
Manchester United v Brentford, Saturday 3pm
Being forced from the field with “stud marks all the way down the back of his calf” after a clash with Tottenham’s Mohammed Kudus towards the end of last weekend’s match led to Leif Davis missing his first Premier League minutes of the season. It left Ipswich’s central defensive pairing of Issa Diop and Dara O’Shea as their only players to have been on the pitch for the entirety of the league campaign so far. O’Shea said this week of playing with Diop that “the more games we play with each other, obviously the better we’ll become as a pair”. They’re being given the best possible chance, even if Ipswich are yet to keep a clean sheet and have already conceded 22 goals, from an opposition xG of 21.82. Only the league’s bottom two have conceded a higher xG. More surprising is that Aston Villa have the next highest tally, with 18.56. Tuesday, when Villa lost 1-0 at Galatasaray, marked out a month since their last win. They have drawn three and scored in only two of their six outings. Ipswich may be just two points and two places outside the bottom three, but a win would put these teams level. SB
Ipswich v Aston Villa, Saturday 5.30pm
“We are having a great week,” Virgil van Dijk said after Liverpool followed up their 4-0 dismantling of Manchester United with a 3-0 win at Club Brugge that reinforced the strides being made by Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz and Andoni Iraola’s team overall. Liverpool’s week contrasts starkly with their local rivals. Everton suffered the heaviest defeat and produced arguably the worst performance of David Moyes’s second spell in charge on Monday when going down 4-0 at Brentford. James Tarkowski’s red card made no difference, so superior were Keith Andrews’s side from the start, but the absence of the Everton captain could be keenly felt on Sunday. Liverpool won the first Merseyside derby at Hill Dickinson Stadium last season from a 100th-minute corner, capitalising on disruption to Everton’s central defence when Jarrad Branthwaite went off injured. Without Tarkowski the hosts may be vulnerable again. Jake O’Brien could get his long-awaited chance to stake a claim as Branthwaite’s partner in the most demanding circumstances. Andy Hunter

items.title: Hearts' European hopes hang by a thread but Vrancken proud
items.summary:
Hearts' European hopes hang by a thread but Vrancken proud
- Published
There was a bittersweet feeling at Tynecastle after Folarin Balogun's 94th-minute winner preserved Monaco's perfect Conference League record and condemned Hearts to a third defeat from four.
Wouter Vrancken's side had gone toe-to
items.text:
Hearts' European hopes hang by a thread but Vrancken proud
- Published
There was a bittersweet feeling at Tynecastle after Folarin Balogun's 94th-minute winner preserved Monaco's perfect Conference League record and condemned Hearts to a third defeat from four.
Wouter Vrancken's side had gone toe-to-toe with one of the best teams in the tournament, scored two glorious goals, but ultimately came away with nothing for their efforts.
Now they have little to no margin for error in their two remaining league phase matches.
They will likely have to beat both Borac Banja Luka of Bosnia and Cyprus' Pafos to reach the knockout stages, but if they perform as they did against Monaco, they will give themselves a fighting chance.
Hearts have garnered a reputation as entertainers under Vrancken - scoring a raft of goals while being porous at the back.
This game was their season in microcosm. The goals - scored by Jordi Altena and Sabah Kerjota - were things of beauty, picture-perfect strikes worthy of any stage.
But as thrilling as Hearts were in attack, they were as baffling at the back.
Jamie McCart unnecessarily tripped Matthis Abline, allowing Balogun to score from the penalty spot and Monaco's second came from Altena giving the ball away.
"It's Gladiators - are we not entertained? It's sensational," said Hearts legend John Robertson at half-time, with the game finely poised at 2-2.
'Biggest thing is pride in performance'
Both teams had chances to win it in the second half, but it was Monaco who took theirs in the final stages. Mamadou Coulibaly was afforded too much space and he slipped Balogun through to beat Beau Reus.
"It's a lack of nous and a little bit of naivety," former Hearts midfielder Michael Stewart said on TNT Sports. "McCart backs off and allows the ball to be played into Balogun's feet."
Despite the frustrating nature of the late concession, Vrancken's overwhelming emotion was of pride.
"I'm very disappointed with how we give the goal away at the end," he said.
"The biggest thing is the pride for the performance today. Against a side of Monaco's [quality] - we're still missing nine players through injury - this performance was really pleasing."
Before the recent international break, Hearts were beaten 3-1 by Swiss outfit Thun, before a shock 5-2 home defeat by high-flying Falkirk in the Scottish Premiership.
However, they bounced back with a ruthless 8-0 win at Dundee on Saturday and carried that confidence into this game against a team with a far bigger budget.
"You saw that the confidence was there from the weekend and there was conviction around their box," Vrancken added. "It will not work every time, but the conviction and energy was there again.
"Our team kept their heads in the game and kept going for it, not being pleased with 2-2. Really pleased with what I saw."
Aside from his dismay at Balogun's winner and how it came about, Vrancken's main gripe was with the officials.
He felt there was a foul on Kerjota in the build-up to Monaco's second goal and was bemused at the fact neither Takumi Minamino and Denis Zakaria were sent off.
Minamino - already on a yellow card - wiped out Sabri Guendouz on the edge of the Monaco box, but got away with a warning. And VAR opted not to intervene after Zakaria went over the top of the ball and caught Pierre Landry Kabore on the shin.
"The second goal, they pulled Sabah [Kerjota] and he can't do his defensive work," Vrancken said.
"It was not the only refereeing decision that was interesting tonight. I don't know how it's possible not to give a red card for the tackle on [Pierre Landry Kabore]. It's clearly above the ankle, so it's always a red card.
"And why didn't Minamino get a second yellow before half-time? He prevents a shot from Sabri at the edge of the box.
"The explanation of the fourth official was even more crazy - he explained it could be for his first yellow card, but not for his second yellow. It was clearly a yellow card and then we were against 10 in the second half."

The winner will automatically qualify for the 2027 Women's World Cup in Brazil.
"I always respect every oppon
items.text:
MANSFIELD, Texas -- United States women's national team head coach Emma Hayes said she expects El Salvador to play "the game of their lives" in Friday's Concacaf W Championship quarterfinal.
The winner will automatically qualify for the 2027 Women's World Cup in Brazil.
"I always respect every opponent, and you have to start with that," Hayes told reporters on Thursday at Texas Health Mansfield Stadium. "I think if you start looking at things like rankings, then you prime your brain to say things like, 'Oh, it's going to be an easy game.'
"More often than not, from my experiences, they end up being more challenging for lots of reasons. First of all, for El Salvador, this is going to be the game of their lives. They get the opportunity to qualify for the World Cup."
El Salvador are ranked No. 78 in the world and making their first appearance at the Concacaf W Championship after winning their pre-qualifying group.
The United States has qualified for all nine previous Women's World Cups and won four of them, more than any other country. The Americans are ranked second in the world behind Spain and are one of the contenders to win the 2027 edition. They are also the reigning Olympic champions.
"They have a lot of pride, and they want to perform for their country," Hayes said about El Salvador. "There's something at stake, and because of that, it's not a friendly game. And disrupting a team like the United States it might not be going toe-to-toe with us in certain parts of the game, but making it difficult for us? One hundred percent I think that will be the case."
Hayes praised El Salvador's ability to create opportunities in counterattacks and one-v-one opportunities. She also pointed to El Salvador's threat on set pieces.
Earlier in the day at training, U.S. captain Lindsey Heaps told ESPN and a small group of reporters that there is more game footage of Concacaf opponents than in previous cycles, which allows for more specific preparation.
Heaps echoed Hayes, saying that "we do not take any of these games lightly," and that the team prepared for El Salvador like they did for matches against world No. 1 Spain last month.
U.S. forward Sophia Wilson said that each game is like a final, which is good preparation for the World Cup.
"Any Concacaf tournament, we know it's going to be a challenge in a different way," Wilson said. "It's going to be maybe a little bit of a chaotic game, but I think that's a good test for us."
Hayes told reporters at Saturday's NWSL Championship in Washington, D.C., that she was excited to finally have the opportunity to start the self-proclaimed "Triple Espresso" of Wilson, Trinity Rodman and Mallory Swanson together for the first time since the 2024 Olympics.
About an hour later, in the opening minutes of the Washington Spirit's 2-1 loss to the Kansas City Current, Rodman was tackled hard and injured her shoulder.
Rodman stayed in the match and scored the Spirit's lone goal in second-half stoppage time. She said after the game that her shoulder felt "phenomenal," but U.S. Soccer announced earlier this week that Rodman would miss World Cup qualifying. She was replaced on the roster by forward Jaedyn Shaw.
"For Trin, she took a pretty hard hit," Hayes said on Thursday. "She was pretty beat up after the game. This happens, and unfortunately, she's not fit for this camp, but I'm sure she will be back by January."
Also absent from the U.S. roster is forward and attacking midfielder Pietra Tordin, who earned her first call-up and first cap last month against Spain. Tordin is training with Brazil in Japan during this international window. She holds dual citizenship with the U.S. and Brazil and has played for both countries at the youth international level.
"She was with us, and obviously she's got Brazilian heritage.," Hayes said. "She's going to train with Brazil. No more than that, so she's not cap-tied. I understand. It was a conversation that I've had, particularly with her agent, and yeah, there's no more to be said on it."
El Salvador's federation announced earlier this week that it would pay the players a $1 million shared bonus if they qualify for the World Cup for the first time.
The losers of the four Concacaf quarterfinals will get second chances at qualification in play-in games next week. The two winners of those matches will advance to next year's FIFA global playoff, where the final World Cup berths will be secured.
"Process is a really, really, really heavy word," El Salvador head coach Erick Acuña told reporters on Friday. "We are just trying to go step by step. And every step that we made, we have to be really secure. But we don't want to dream; we want to do.
"At the end of everything, we have to believe in step by step, because I don't want to be lucky. I just want to be secure that we are going to be in these stages all the time, and the only way to do it is believe. We have to believe in our process but inside of the process, there's a lot of things that we have to do. We have to invest. Without investment, there is no progression."

items.text:
Bournemouth's dream Europa League start continued on Thursday as the south-coast club set a new record for a debuting English club in Europe.
Marco Rose's side fought back from a goal down in Spain against Celta Vigo to win 2-1 and extend their perfect start to the competition to five games.
- Europa League game halted amid police clashes over fans' Palestine banner
They are the first English club in history to win their first five European games and are only the third team ever in major European competitions to achieve that feat, after Nürnberg in 1961-62 and Ararat in 1972-73.
It was also a club-record extending 10th straight win in all competitions for Marco Rose's side, who sit an impressive fifth in the Premier League.
Thursday's win, which keeps them top of the Europa League league phase table, was made all the more impressive by the fact it came after playing for more than an hour with 10 men following Bafodé Diakité's red card in the 23rd minute.
"We showed a lot of character," Bournemouth's Amine Adli TNT Sport. "It's amazing to come back in this way and go back home with the three points.
"I think it was down to the mentality of the players. From the moment we conceded the goal, and even after the red card, we always believed in ourselves.
"What's fantastic is that in the dressing room, even before the coach started speaking, everybody was saying, 'we can do this.' Everyone was motivated and still believed we could turn things around."
Adli's cross shortly after time set up Álvaro Rodríguez to head an equalising goal, turning the tables on Celta after they had gone in at halftime a goal up and a man up.
"I was looking for someone in the box," Adli added. "I know Alvaro is very good in the air and he was in a good position so I just tried to deliver a dangerous ball towards the far post."
The visitors looked in trouble when, minutes after Iago Aspas had curled Celta in front, Diakité was red-carded for a poorly timed tackle.
Rodríguez's goal then set the tone for an excellent second half in which Rose's team were comfortably the better side despite their numerical disadvantage.
Substitute Rayan swept in the winner 12 minutes from time to give Bournemouth one foot into the knockout rounds.
Information from ESPN Global Research and PA contributed to this report.

items.title: Kimmich slams 'not Bayern-like' treatment of Musiala amid health row
items.summary:
Bayern Munich midfielder Joshua Kimmich has launched a stinging attack on the club's "not Bayern-like" treatment of his teammate Jamal Musiala, who has a condition which causes seizures.
Senior Bayern figures have publicly questioned Musiala's performances and contract after repeated seizures caused
items.text:
Bayern Munich midfielder Joshua Kimmich has launched a stinging attack on the club's "not Bayern-like" treatment of his teammate Jamal Musiala, who has a condition which causes seizures.
Senior Bayern figures have publicly questioned Musiala's performances and contract after repeated seizures caused by a neurological condition, including two on the field in preseason games, drawing protests from players' union FIFPRO.
Now a key player has spoken out, too, and warned Bayern risks undermining its family image.
"What I don't understand is the way this is being communicated in public," Kimmich told reporters after Bayern's 2-1 Champions League loss at Lille on Wednesday.
"It must never happen that the burden is placed on a player. The club is obviously the top priority and bigger than a player, but it's not bigger than a person. That's an absolute no-go and it is not Bayern-like either."
Kimmich also questioned whether Musiala's run of injuries over the last two years, including a badly fractured leg at the Club World Cup last year, had more impact on his game than the neurological condition.
"It's not the case that he has problems because he's unprofessional. He's there every day trying to get the maximum out of himself," Kimmich added.
Bayern met with Musiala's agents Tuesday and clarified the timeline of events, dismissing speculation Musiala could have concealed the condition when he signed his last contract extension.
Bayern said the club and Musiala's representatives both accept he was first examined for seizure symptoms in April 2025, two months after the contract extension.
"This took place in consultation with FC Bayern and its medical unit immediately after the neurological symptoms first appeared," Bayern said.
Musiala went public with his diagnosis in August after collapsing on the field in two preseason games, leaving players and fans alarmed.
- Bayern Munich, Jamal Musiala mess shows German champs at their worst
- Bayern Munich: Jamal Musiala's health 'top priority' amid contract doubts
- Injury-hit Bayern beaten by Lille to suffer first UCL loss
Bayern coach Vincent Kompany said at the time the incidents were triggered by a change in the medication Musiala was taking. Musiala was rested for the start of the season and has since missed several games with a muscle issue.
Musiala came off the bench in the 76th minute of Bayern's loss at Lille, which continued a bad week for Bayern.
Ballon D'Or winner Harry Kane injured his ankle Friday and faces months on the sidelines, while Bayern have lost the lead in the Bundesliga to Borussia Dortmund and have now slipped to 15th in the Champions League standings.
